#4891. ‘I Signed Up for a Marathon at the Worst Possible Time—And It Was the Best Decision I Made’

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

“If you wait until you feel ready, you’ll be waiting forever.”

I wasn’t planning on running a marathon this year, let alone the New York City Marathon. Between its notoriously hilly course, relentless bridges, and the logistics of traveling across the country from my home in Colorado, NYC wasn’t exactly the easiest to take on. I’m also a busy mama to a 3½-year-old and 2-year-old, I work full time (I am the founding coach of the Ladder app and coach Team Body and Bell), and I had sinus surgery about six months ago. A marathon definitely wasn’t on my bingo card among the trenches of motherhood—but it happened.

After a really healthy and injury-free training block, I made it to the starting line. It was time for me to have my redemptive victory, but instead, I rolled up with the flu. At the time, I had no idea, and I chalked up how lousy I was feeling to the exhaustion of traveling with two little kids, lack of sleep, and all the chaos that comes with it. It wasn’t until I got home and was diagnosed that I realized what I’d actually been dealing with on race day. From the starting line, I found myself self-loathing and robbed of the marathon experience I’d worked so hard for.

But little did I know, the setbacks and imperfections of race day and training were actually going to allow me to experience the marathon even more than if I had been chasing a pace and finish time.

Between two pregnancies and postpartum periods, a C-section, and other unplanned health setbacks, it had been a difficult few years. I felt constantly defeated. Even as someone who works in fitness, I felt like I hadn’t done much to take care of myself in quite some time.

When the marathon opportunity presented itself, there was something almost rebellious about being able to choose my own hard in spite of the daily challenges that were out of my control as a mom.

As I was flooded with mom guilt, I kept asking myself: When will it be a good time to do this? When is it a good time to do anything for yourself as a mom? The answer was a resounding never. So I decided to rip off the bandaid, find a bib (thank you, Gatorade!), and fully commit to a three-month training block with a coach. (I hired a Body and Bell member who had actually trained with me since the start of the app. She is a seven-time NYC Marathoner and the most passionate running coach I know. Check her out on Instagram: @lindaleighlore.)

My life did not stop during this time. Work was more demanding than ever. We went on two family vacations. The kids got me sick multiple times. The training conditions were never perfect—but I did manage to get the mileage in. I reminded myself of something I say as a coach all the time: “It doesn’t need to be perfect, it just needs to be done.”

Let me preface something important as someone who works in fitness: endurance training was very new to me. I am a speed, power, and strength girlie at heart. The three-hour-plus long runs, pounding the pavement and moving slower, was very mentally unstimulating and out of my comfort zone.

But this new sport allowed me to enter a headspace I had never experienced before. There was something so recharging about being able to leave the house, put my phone in my pocket, and be in my own thoughts that healed me in ways I didn’t know I needed to be healed. Training did not only provide a break from the kids, but it also gave me a space to allow me to become more available for them.

In the fitness world, running and strength training are often viewed as two completely different styles of training. We have strength versus cardio zealots. But what more people need to understand is how much they thrive together.

The aerobic engine I was building with running gave me more cardio capacity for my lifts (lifting heavier felt smoother than it ever had) and all the muscle I had gained over the years made me an extremely strong and resilient runner (I recovered so well in between runs).

I felt structurally and aerobically unstoppable.

When I got to the start line, I knew something was off. I grew up as an athlete and knew what to expect with the competition nerves—but this was different. I was coughing, had a sore throat, and a raging headache. I kept telling myself it would all go away once I started moving. And for a while, it did. But around mile six, somewhere deep in Brooklyn, the symptoms came back with a vengeance, along with full-body chills.

It was way too early to be “bonking” in a marathon, and I was confused and simply annoyed. I tried to stay toward the middle of the street, away from the crowds. I purposely didn’t wear headphones to take in the crowd’s energy, yet there I was, trying to hide from it.

I crossed the Queensboro Bridge into Manhattan, where I knew my family was waiting for me at mile 17. I was so excited to see them, but I was also dragging so badly by this point, and I needed to take a quick break. I quickly took some medicine, gave some hugs, and kept trekking on.

I knew the only way out was through. I focused on one mile at a time, kept taking my gel, and tried to stay positive. Thankfully, that's the beautiful thing about a major marathon: There are reasons all around you to keep pushing. Everywhere I turned, I saw people of all ages, backgrounds, and abilities, with their own reasons for being out there. It was impossible not to feel inspired—or reminded that I was part of something so much bigger than my own race.It wasn’t until mile 22, shockingly on the Fifth Avenue climb to Central Park, where I had a breakthrough that felt supernatural—a combo of adrenaline and gratitude for what my body was doing. I was able to see my family one last time and then finish the race strong.

I was expecting to cross the finish line feeling so victorious, maybe even relieved that it was over. But I felt kind of disappointed. Not because of how I’d performed, but because this thing I’d spent months training for, thinking about, and looking forward to was suddenly over.

So let me be the first to tell you that what you get out of a marathon has very little to do with how fast you finish. And that's not to take anything away from people who work incredibly hard to get faster and faster in this sport. That's amazing! But the marathon is the great equalizer, and here's what I mean.

The marathon is hard for everyone. It doesn’t matter how fast you run it or whether it’s your first marathon or your 10th. There's a camaraderie that develops on the course because everyone is going through something so taxing together. You're all hurting, you're all pushing through, and your pace doesn't change that.

Plus, no two marathons are the same: different climates, crowds, elevations, and race-day challenges (like getting sick!). Your finish time cannot possibly capture everything you experienced out there. And it certainly doesn't always reflect the months of hard work you put into training or what you're actually capable of.

Then there's the sheer physical demand of the distance. A marathon requires so much time on your feet. You have to have a fueling strategy (salt…hydration…carbs…). No matter your pace, 26.2 miles is going to take it all out of you.

But maybe the most incredible part is that everyone out there is running for a different reason. You will see people out there of all ages, with limb differences, on wheels, with vision impairments, pregnant, pausing mid-race to breastfeed, after a weight-loss transformation. You name it. Everyone has a story, which makes the marathon one of the most inspiring environments you get to run in.

Bandit Running Women's Vanisher™ V-Neck Race Crop

My point with all of this: If you wait until you feel ready, you’ll be waiting forever.

If you want to get better at running, dabble in a 5K or 10K, or even a half-marathon. But if you want to learn who you really are deep within your core, sign up for the marathon. There's something about those 26.2 miles that shows you a side of yourself you might never have met otherwise. But you have to surrender to every mile and let the race have its way with you to truly transform.

And if you’re a busy mama like me—debating if you can, debating if it’s fair to the kids, debating if it’s the right time—there is no right time. There will always be a sick kid, a work deadline, a setback, a reason to wait. You aren’t promised to show up to the start line feeling your best.

Not because you have anything to prove. You get through bedtime every night without a crowd cheering you on or a medal waiting at the finish line. You're already doing hard things every single day. But sometimes you need to choose something hard just for you to remember what you're capable of.

And maybe the best part isn't even what you discover about yourself along the way. It's that your kids get to grow up watching their mom go after something she wants, even when the timing isn't perfect, even when it's hard, and even when it would be so much easier not to.

Lauren Kanski, CPT, is a member of the Women’s Health advisory board, a NASM-certified personal trainer, and a kettlebell and strength training specialist. She is the founding coach of the Ladder fitness app, where she leads Team Body and Bell, a strength training program focused on building muscle, power, and confidence. She lives in Colorado with her husband and two little ones.

#4890. Reformation’s Debut Home Collection Gives French Rugs an LA Attitude

For years, people shopping at Reformation have asked about something the brand didn’t sell. “One of the biggest comments that we get is that the stores look so beautiful and the rugs are amazing,” says Lauren Caris Cohan, the brand’s chief creative officer. Typically, she says, one question follows that observation: “Where can we get them?” Until now, the answer was nowhere; Thomas Coccimiglio, founder of the French rugmaker Les Editions de Tapis, is “really precious” about his designs for Reformation stores, Cohan says, and doesn’t reuse them for other clients.

Today, Reformation’s collaboration with Les Editions de Tapis makes the coveted rugs available to the public, with nine limited-edition styles, all made to order and priced between $1,000 and $5,000.

Long before he began outfitting Reformation showrooms, Coccimiglio spent more than 15 years as a textile designer in fashion, working in London, Paris, and New York. At Tory Burch, his trips to meet embroiderers in Italy and India eventually led him to rug-making, and during the pandemic, he left fashion for interiors, though his fashion background continues to influence him, even in the way he speaks about rugs: “I approach a rug almost as I would a piece of embroidery on a garment.”

Reformation opens more than 15 stores a year, Cohan says, and each one gets its own hand-sketched motif and custom colorway from Coccimiglio. “There’s a bit of a French sense of humor, a bone-dry sense of humor, in our [Reformation] brand DNA,” Cohan says, “that’s reflected in Thomas’ designs.”

For the new capsule collection of rugs, Reformation gave Coccimiglio full creative direction. The conversations that launched the collaboration involved Marie Antoinette, swans, a lot of pink and blue—all components also reflected in the partnering 12-piece clothing campaign, live today. To help inspire a cohesive thread linking Coccimiglio’s line to the ethos of the brand, he also revisited years of store designs for details to incorporate. “There’s something nostalgic about these pieces, almost like a little Proustian madeleine,” Coccimiglio says. “For customers who have experienced Reformation's stores over the years, these pieces might feel strangely familiar, almost iconic.”

The Chintz rugs set two crossed palm trees (Cohan’s idea, which Coccimiglio sketched by hand) between trailing vine borders, with herons and swans tucked at their roots. Swans Fans puts two black-outlined swans among spiky fan palms on a French blue foundation. Le Chat leaves a field of lilac almost entirely empty, save for one striped cat walking a broken black line. Le Classique has an ivory ground, two wavering oxblood borders, and a single dot, fitting anyone with French sensibilities sans menagerie.

The rugs are hand-knotted from wool, silk, and linen. Coccimiglio manufactures his larger pieces in India, where he finds the wool softer and better suited to big formats. Smaller editions come from Nepal, where Himalayan wool is denser, and the results are ornate, “like jewelry,” says Coccimiglio. While you could find a less expensive rug elsewhere, Cohan points out that Coccimiglio’s are designed for longevity of use—plus, the rugmaker’s own work outside the Reformation collaboration costs considerably more. “This is a much more accessible price point for something so detailed and so custom,” she says.

Cohan, who restores midcentury houses in Los Angeles with her husband Matt Jacoby under the name Bob Audrey, doesn’t picture a single kind of room to house these rugs. “You could have it in a midcentury house in the Hollywood Hills, but it also would look so stunning in [a] herringbone-floor apartment in New York City,” she says.

The campaign was shot in a house at the top of Wonderland Park in Laurel Canyon, a 1950s enclave of single-story midcentury houses that includes Pierre Koenig’s Case Study House No. 21. Coccimiglio, meanwhile, works from a 17th-century hôtel particulier in Dijon. It’s fitting that the premise of the collection enmeshes old-world France with modern LA, as Coccimiglio places his work “somewhere between these two worlds: French heritage and contemporary culture.”

The collection is available to shop on Reformation.com on Nov. 9.

#4887. How a Society Photographer Fell in Love With an Unexpected Upstate Victorian Home

I had no intention of buying the house on Willard Place. I only added it to the short list of Hudson properties I planned to visit out of sheer morbid curiosity. The house looked completely crazy online, with its wild colors and eccentric embellishments, inside and out—a confounding mix of hideous and fabulous. I felt compelled to check it out in person. Real estate agent extraordinaire Julia Crowley made the appointment at Willard the first stop on our house-hunting itinerary. The artist Helen Marden, a dear friend and owner of the nearby Hotel Tivoli, decided to come along for the ride. “What are we doing here?” she asked when we got out of the car. I’d forgotten to mention this purely voyeuristic side trip.

The polychrome exterior of Craig-Martin's house in Hudson, New York.

Craig-Martin on the front steps of her home with her beloved Roo, a whippet and chihuahua mix.

Above the mantel hangs a painting by Haitian artist Ramphis Magloire. To the left is an etching by Brice Marden, a gift from the artist to Craig-Martin’s son on the occasion of his birth. To the right is a Fernand Léger print, a gift from the homeowner’s artist father, Michael Craig-Martin. A mix of Indian, Moroccan, Italian, Chinese, and Indonesian art and furnishings testifies to a well-traveled life.

I was fully expecting the polychrome Victorian house to be crammed full of furniture, as seen in the online listing. But when Helen, Julia, and I stepped in, it was breathtakingly empty, save for shafts of winter sunlight that illuminated the generous rooms and old wood floors. It became clear that the grotesque furniture I’d seen in the photos was virtual—a terrifying misuse of AI. We sat on the old iron radiators, quietly absorbing the beautiful proportions and unexpected calm. It was fabulous—that was undeniable—but with five bedrooms, it was far more house than I was looking for, and seemed daunting for one person. Helen disagreed. At the next stop, she took one look at the house from the car and didn’t bother to get out.

Craig-Martin seated on a chaise on the terrace off the dining room. A painting by Joe Brainard hangs above a vase from Regan & Smith in Hudson, New York.

George Nakashima chairs surround a table from India made of dismantled boat parts.

An Indonesian stool sits beside a rattan chaise beneath an Indian elephant mobile on the terrace.

A barracuda sculpture by Dalwa Donoffre rests on an Aalto stool in the window bay of the dining room. Beside it, an Ashley Bickerton sculpture sits on a marble pedestal from Rajasthan, surrounded by Stone Age tools, a whale vertebra, and a turquoise bowl by Mary Heilmann.

In the entry hall, a Josef Albers print is installed above a rustic table with a Cameroonian fertility figure.

Over the following months I continued looking in the area, but nothing struck a chord. “You should be thinking about Willard,” Helen kept saying. “It’s a good house.” Completed in 1875, the classic Victorian was built during the whaling boom that enriched Hudson and dotted the town with other equally eccentric Victorian homes replete with multiple bow windows, terraces, and turrets. It had been standing empty and neglected for years, but a thorough assessment did not threaten any looming “old house” disasters. Unable to get the beauty of the place out of my mind, I made an offer.

An ant sculpture from Deyrolle in Paris joins an array of copper pans in the kitchen.

A pastel drawing by Finbar Craig-Martin hangs above a Chinese console table with bagel sculptures by Hanna Liden.

I enlisted a friend to help me move in, though furniture would have to come later. We drove up from the city in a rented van filled with Moroccan rugs and two inflatable mattresses, and ate pizza on the floor in front of a roaring fire. Two years later, I can’t imagine living without the house’s spaciousness and light, or its grand old-world flourishes. Frankly, I don’t know how I coped for so many years without a Norma Desmond staircase. It seems unrealistic now to imagine life without one, which confirms my suspicion that luxury is a one-way trip.

Artworks in the primary bedroom include (clockwise from far left) a painting by Michael Craig-Martin, a painting by Charlie Lucas (above mantel), a light sculpture by Theo Rosenblum (on mantel), a Jessica Craig-Martin photograph of Fran Lebowitz (floor), and a round painting on glass by Finbar Craig-Martin.

A crayon drawing of the homeowner at age two by her mother, Jan Hashey, sits on a Balinese child’s chair in the bathroom.

Jessica Craig-Martin in the bedroom of her son, Finbar. To the right of a movie poster from Ghana is a photograph by Jason Noyes.

Craig-Martin’s son’s room has a Paul McCobb desk, an Eames chair modified by artists Eric Wesley and Piero Golia. and a poster of Ursula Andress from the movie Dr. No above a rustic kitchen cabinet.

In Finbar’s room, a Nate Lowman pizza painting hangs beside a foam-core cutout of David Bowie.

I added a red refrigerator and stove to match the kitchen’s vintage red Formica countertops, and a lifetime’s worth of art and ephemera, from artwork by my parents and friends to artifacts, textiles, and natural oddities collected on various travels. There are unnatural oddities, too. For example, I have a weakness for cheap Japanese plushy cushions, my favorite being a huge pink peach that, when viewed from a certain angle, morphs unmistakably into a huge pink ass. It is also evident that I favor crocodiles and alligators in any form, though if you asked me why, I couldn’t say. One thing is certain: We are a very long way from “form follows function.” Fortunately, at least to my eye, the house absorbed my proclivity for both the ridiculous and the sublime with grace. Helen was right. It is a good house, and it has welcomed me, perhaps recognizing in me a madness that in some way matches its own.

The home office/library features an Alvar Aalto chair and stool, a low alligator table Craig-Martin found on the street in New York City, and a totem from the Solomon Islands displayed beside the fireplace. #4885. Progressive Overload Training: What It Means, Benefits, And How To Do It, According To Trainers

Understanding this concept is a must to build muscle, trainers agree.

If you’ve ever Googled “how to gain muscle?” there is no doubt the term “progressive overload” popped up. At its core, progressive overload training is a style of strength training where you gradually increase the amount of stress placed on your body during exercise. But what does that really even mean?

If you want to build bigger muscles, lose weight, and/or lift heavy, you have to gradually place more load and stress on the body to force that initial change and growth in the muscle fiber, explains Kendra Madigan a personal trainer at Physical Equilibrium. Progressive overload training is the way to do that, she adds.

Meet the experts: Kendra Madigan is a dancer and certified personal trainer at Physical Equilibrium. Kate Georgiadis, the founder of LIFT, a New York based fitness initiative.

This article will delve into why progressive overload training works and how to implement it into your routine—along with expert tips on how to prevent injury. Plus, you'll get a four-week full-body training plan designed by Kate Georgiadis, the founder of LIFT, a New York-based fitness initiative focused on empowering women through individual and group training.

With progressive overload training, you want to gradually increase the amount of stress your body experiences during exercise to increase your strength. “This can be achieved by increasing the weight, repetitions, frequency, or intensity of exercises,” says Georgiadis, who explains that this style of training forces the body to adapt to a higher tension than it has previously withstood.

During exercise, your muscles will tear slightly, Madigan says. When the tears heal, it makes the muscle bigger. “So if you’re not lifting heavy enough, you’re not going to get that progressive result that you’re looking for,” she says. However, if you progress too fast and don’t give your muscles time to heal these tiny tears, you risk injury.

So what’s the sweet spot when it comes to increasing weight? For your baseline, you want to begin with a manageable load. “If you think, ‘I can probably do 15 pounds’—start with 10 or 12.5 and make sure you can [manage] that,” says Madigan, “Always start low and go high.”

Next, you want to incorporate incremental load increases. This can look different for everyone, depending on how fast your body is adapting, your experience level, and the frequency you work out.

Increasing the number of reps or volume is one way to bump up your load, but that can become time-consuming as it requires you to lengthen your workout time, so increasing weight tends to be the more common route people take. “For a beginner who starts tracking their weights, the best approach is to keep consistent parameters. Trying to change the reps, weights, and sets each week can be confusing,” says Georgiadis. “I suggest keeping the reps and sets the same over the first four weeks and trying to increase the weight while maintaining proper form.”

To do this, once you can perform your current workout and move your current load with proper form easily, up the weight by 2-5 percent, she recommends. This could be a weekly or biweekly increase, or based on performance and feel.

If you want to go by feel, Madigan recommends doing sets of eight to 12 reps where you are at exhaustion for the last two reps. “You’re going for that exhaustion phase, so that’s how you judge where your weight should be,” she says. Some trainers call this phase “to failure,” but Madigan prefers the word exhaustion. “If you can only do five reps of something, take the weight down a little bit, build your strength until you can get at least 10 reps in, with the last two reps going to exhaustion,” she explains.

Georgiadis gauges when her clients should bump up their weight by having them do a few extra reps. “Every week, I usually push my clients to try to get a few more reps with the weight they are using (do 15 reps instead of 12), and if they can do that, I will increase the weight on the next set or in the next session,” she says.

To help visualize what a progressive overload training schedule would look like, Georgiadis designed the sample full-body plan here. But remember, listen to your body and only increase when you can perform the moves for the full amount of reps with the correct form.

Squat: 3 sets of 8 reps with weight about 5 lbs. heavier than week 1

Dumbbell Chest Press: 3 sets of 8 reps with weight about 2.5 lbs. heavier than week 1

Deadlift: 3 sets of 8 reps with weight about 5 lbs. heavier than week 1

Squat: 3 sets of 8 reps with weight about 5 lbs. heavier than week 2

Dumbbell Chest Press: 3 sets of 8 reps with weight about 2.5 lbs. heavier than week 2

Deadlift: 3 sets of 8 reps with weight about 5 lbs. heavier than week 2

Squat: 3 sets of 9 reps with weight about 10 lbs. heavier than week 1

Dumbbell Chest Press: 3 sets of 9 reps with weight about 5 lbs. heavier than week 1

Deadlift: 3 sets of 9 reps with weight about 10 lbs. heavier than week 1

While you may be tempted to keep pushing to harder and harder resistance every week, it is important to deload during a progressive overload cycle too to prevent overtraining and plateaus. “Deload weeks are periods of reduced training intensity and volume, giving the body time to recover and prepare for more intense training,” says Georgiadis.

She recommends incorporating a deload week every four to eight weeks. She says that she tries to time her clients deload weeks with their vacations so the rest can happen naturally in their routines.

During your fitness journey it can be easy to get stuck in a routine. But if you do the same thing each week you will just maintain your current strength and fitness. In order to improve (get stronger, fitter, lose weight, etc.) you must advance the challenges on your body. Following a progressive overload plan allows you to effectively continue to grow, increasing muscle mass and overall athleticism.

Increasing your intensity too fast is a common cause of injuries, trainers agree. “Allow for rest and recovery, adjusting as needed based on how you feel and perform,” says Georgiadis. “Overtraining can be avoided by listening to your body, ensuring proper nutrition, maintaining hydration, and getting adequate sleep.”

Madigan also says it is important to remember to eat and recover to get the most out of the work you are doing and avoid injury. She explains that when you overtrain, you get more tired and less hungry, “That is just a recipe for an injury,” she says, “So always take the recovery. It’s as important as the workout.”

Beyond taking rest days and listening to your body, there are several other ways to prevent injury while doing a progressive overload style plan. One is by planning your training around your menstrual cycle. The different phases of your cycle can make working out easier and harder, so for some women, a completely linear progressive overload training plan might not work.

“On weeks when hormonal changes make it challenging, it's entirely acceptable not to increase the weight or reps. Instead, you can maintain the current level of intensity and then aim for progression in the following week when you might feel stronger and more capable,” says Georgiadis.

She recommends doing high-intensity workouts and strength training during your follicular phase, doing controlled, linear strength training during ovulation when there is an increased risk of injury, and doing moderate to low intensity exercise during the luteal phase. (Read all about cycle syncing at the link ahead!) “This approach not only respects the body's natural rhythms but also supports sustained progress in training without risking injury or burnout,” she says.

#4884. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

Your underwear is the first thing you put on and the last thing you take off, so it has to work with you, not against you, all day long. If it doesn't do its job, you'll feel it, whether it's discomfort, chafing, or overheating.

Think about it: excellent underwear isn't just about looking cool (though that's like icing on the cake). It's about how it performs in real life. Are you lounging at home? Going for a long run? Stuck on a flight for hours? Each of these scenarios demands something different. You need underwear that supports your lifestyle, whether that's stretch for flexibility, moisture-wicking for sweat, or breathability to keep things fresh down yonder.

The best breathable underwear manages heat and moisture so sweat can escape instead of getting trapped against your skin. Many use micro-knit or mesh-like weaves that create tiny air channels within the fabric, allowing heat to dissipate and air to circulate as you move. Others incorporate moisture-wicking fibers to pull sweat away from the body and spread it across the surface of the fabric so it evaporates faster. Some brands even add targeted “cool zones” or thinner panels in high-sweat areas to boost airflow where you need it most.

When underwear can’t breathe, moisture builds up, leading to overheating, chafing, irritation, and odor. Breathable underwear works with your body by keeping things cooler, drier, and more comfortable throughout the day. For Men’s Health guys, breathability makes a difference for everyday wear, long commutes, desk jobs, workouts, travel days, and humid conditions. It’s especially clutch for guys who sweat easily, live in hot climates, train hard, or spend long stretches in the same pair from morning to night.

As part of the Men’s Health style team, led by our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, I’ve tested some of the best—and worst—underwear on the market firsthand. Since 2015, our team has worn, washed, and stressed-tested more than 100 pairs across every major style, brand, and fabric imaginable, from classic cotton briefs to high-tech performance boxer briefs and luxe everyday upgrades.

Testing wasn't limited to just one body type or fit preference. In addition to my own wear tests, multiple Men's Health editors with different builds pitched in, spanning sizes from small through XXL. This allowed us to see how each pair fit and performed across a wide range of body types, rises, thigh sizes, and proportions—and to flag issues like inconsistent sizing, rolling waistbands, or fabric that only works on one kind of frame.

I wore each pair repeatedly in real-life situations, including workdays, workouts, commutes, travel, and weekend outings. I looked at how each pair performed over time, paying close attention to whether fabrics remained soft without pilling, waistbands held their shape, seams avoided chafing, and support held up after hours of movement. I judged each pair on fabric quality, fit, breathability, odor control, stretch and recovery, durability after repeated washes, and comfort levels ranging from morning to night. Only the pairs that consistently delivered comfort, support, and long-term performance earned a spot on this list. What you’ll find here are the top 12 best men’s underwear options that rose to the top after years of hands-on testing by the Men’s Health team.

Boxers: They’re classic, loose-fitting shorts that are lightweight, with lots of breathing room, and zero restriction. They’re great for lounging or sleeping because they feel airy and relaxed, but that same looseness makes them less practical under slim pants. Fabric can bunch, ride up, and offer little to no support if you’re moving around a lot. Boxer briefs: They’re cut like boxers but fit snugly like briefs. That means they hug your thighs, hold everything in place, and layer smoothly under jeans, trousers, or even gym shorts. They also prevent chafing since the fabric creates a barrier between your thighs—a lifesaver if you walk a lot or hit the gym. The tradeoff? They’re less airy than boxers, but most guys prefer the balance of comfort, coverage, and support.

That really depends on your laundry schedule. If you’re someone who does laundry once a week, aim for at least 10 to 12 pairs so you’ve got a little cushion. If laundry happens less often—say every two weeks—you’ll probably want 15 to 20 pairs. If you’re very active, then consider stocking your drawer with 25 to 30 pairs. Basically, you want enough to last until wash day plus a couple extra for workouts, surprise trips, or the occasional lazy Sunday when you just don’t feel like doing laundry.

A good rule of thumb: it’s reasonable to refresh your stash every six to 12 months, but quality underwear can last longer depending on fabric, frequency of wear, washing, and condition. If the elastic’s shot, they’re sagging, developing holes, or the fabric’s thinning, that’s your cue to toss them. Think of it as a rotation—you don’t need to replace everything at once, but gradually swap in new pairs so you’re always stocked with comfortable, supportive ones.

Every man has worn them at some point; boxers are light and loose and so freeing. They're the classic underwear style for men that feels very relaxed with short legs. This type of underwear is perfect for lounging around the house, sleeping, or wearing under relaxed-fit pants. Also comes in a variety of prints and patterns (hello, personality).

Think speedo. Think upside-down triangle. Briefs provide the required coverage and optimal support while exposing more skin for ease of mobility. Here, there's no risk of leg fabric riding up (because there's none).

Perhaps the most popular one, it's a hybrid of loose-fit boxers and tight briefs, offering a solid balance of support and comfort. If you’re not a fan of underwear that rides up too high, go for boxer briefs that have a longer leg and a snug fit, like compression underwear that’s perfect for the gym. They should skim the leg versus squeezing you too tight.

Like the title says, a trunk is similar to boxer briefs but with a shorter cut—halfway up the thigh. It's best for guys who want something fitted but less fabric around the leg. For some visual assistance, think of trunks as the underwear style that most CK models wear on big billboards.

It depends on personal preference, comfort, and the activity. Here's a quick breakdown to help guide your choice, weighing the pros and cons of both.

Tight underwear (e.g., briefs, boxer briefs) provides better support, which is especially useful for physical activities like running or working out. This type reduces chafing and prevents excessive movement, which can help with comfort throughout the day. Works well under slim-fit pants, as it avoids bunching and creates a cleaner silhouette. If it's too tight, it can restrict airflow and potentially cause discomfort or sweating, especially in warmer weather. Overly tight fits might not be ideal for guys concerned about reproductive health, though the effect is typically negligible with properly sized underwear.

On the other hand, loose underwear is better suited for lounging or casual, low-impact activities since it allows more airflow and freedom of movement. It feels more breathable, making it ideal for hotter climates or relaxed settings. Also, loose underwear can be paired with loose-fit pants for added comfort. This option lacks support, which feel uncomfortable during workouts or physical activity. Plus, it can cramp your style—bunching up under tighter pants and offering a restrictive feel.

If you want to protect the structural integrity of your underwear's waistband, the best way to keep them from stretching is to hand wash them and hang them dry. But given how impractical that is, the second best option is to put them in the washing machine on cold water and use a low dryer setting so the elastic doesn't warp. However, our testers say that most of the pairs they've tried have kept their waistbands' shapes even after several trips to the laundromat. If your underwear's waistband has lost its shape, you're probably overdue to replace it.

Even the best underwear won’t last if you don’t take care of it properly. Washing underwear inside out helps remove sweat and bacteria more effectively while protecting the fabric’s surface. Cold or warm water is usually best, as hot water can break down elastic fibers and cause shrinkage over time. Skip harsh detergents and fabric softeners, especially for performance or moisture-wicking underwear. Softeners can coat fibers and reduce breathability and odor control. When possible, air-drying is ideal, as high heat from dryers is the fastest way to kill stretch and warp waistbands. If you do use a dryer, stick to low heat.

#4879. Michael Strahan Shares the Words That Helped His Daughter Through Brain Cancer Treatment

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Michael Strahan appeared in commercials for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, delivering a message he never imagined would become so personal: “No parent should have to hear that their child has cancer.”

But in 2023, the beloved TV host and former NFL player faced that reality when his daughter, Isabella, was diagnosed with brain cancer at 19 years old.

“[That] line that I used to deliver, usually at the end of the commercial…here I am actually filling that line in my life in real time,” Strahan told Healthline.

Strahan believes his longtime connection with St. Jude was more than a coincidence. After years of advocating for families affected by childhood cancer, he found himself on the other side of that experience.

“When I needed that family…they were there for me,” he said. “I’m just appreciative, and I think things come back to you; give out good, good comes back.”

In October 2023, Isabella began experiencing vomiting, headaches, and balance issues during her freshman year at the University of Southern California (USC). Tests revealed that she had medulloblastoma, a fast-growing cancerous brain tumor located in the cerebellum. She underwent emergency brain surgery, radiation therapy, and four rounds of chemotherapy.

While medulloblastoma typically occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 9, it can also affect young adults like Isabella.

“[The] biology in adolescents and young adults can differ meaningfully from pediatric cases, requiring specialized expertise at centers of excellence for this disease,” Arnab Chakravarti, MD, director of the Brain Tumor Program at The Ohio State University, told Healthline.

Medulloblastoma is sometimes confused with glioblastoma, the most common type of malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma is particularly aggressive, with a median overall survival of just 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.

However, Chakravarti explained that medulloblastoma has a significantly higher cure rate than glioblastoma.

“[This is] a point of genuine hope that deserves to be communicated clearly,” he said.

Radiation therapy is a cornerstone of medulloblastoma treatment. Isabella received proton therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

“For medulloblastoma, this physical precision is transformative,” Chakravarti said. “Proton craniospinal irradiation dramatically reduces [collateral] exposure — preserving cochlear function and hearing, reducing cardiovascular risk, protecting the thyroid, and most critically, sparing developing brain tissue in ways that translate into measurably better neurocognitive outcomes years after treatment.”

He added that multiple prospective studies have shown that children and young adults treated with proton craniospinal irradiation experience less cognitive decline and better quality of life compared to those treated with conventional radiation.

Today, Isabella is back at USC, embracing the everyday routines she once had to put on hold.

“I am back at USC, so…it’s been great, in the midst of exams, so it’s a little stressful, but I actually [am] inviting the stress in because at one point I didn’t have exams, so I’m happy to be back,” Isabella told Healthline.

Along with attending classes, Isabella is enjoying activities such as working out and cooking. She continues to undergo MRI scans of her head and spine every three months, but said that after another year, the scans will become less frequent, occurring every six months.

“But really…I don’t have a lot of doctor’s appointments,” she said.

“It feels like a brand-new life, but it’s a good one. And that’s wonderful,” Isabella said.

Isabella said her family’s support played an important role in helping her through cancer treatment. Spending so much time together in the hospital brought them closer as they watched movies and played cards and board games to pass the time.

“[It] really, really bonds you to people, and just having my dad and my whole family there was something that [you] can’t beat,” she told Healthline.

Michael said that despite the difficult circumstances, he cherishes the time he spent with his daughter. Before her diagnosis, Isabella was a typical teenager who spent much of her time at school or with friends.

“They say you spend the most time with your kid for the first few years of their life, and then once school starts, you don’t get a chance to spend as much time as you would like with them,” he said.

While Michael said he and Isabella already had a close relationship, her diagnosis brought the family even closer and helped them reflect on what mattered most.

“[What] was really important was family, and relationships, and the love that you have for each other, and the support you have to give each other,” he said. “I think that our relationship now is better than ever.”

Today, Michael makes an effort to visit Isabella at USC whenever he’s in Los Angeles during the NFL season.

“Some weekends she [has time for me]. Some she doesn’t,” he said. “But just to have that relationship with your child, where they want to hang out with you, is a good feeling, and that’s the relationship that we have.”

Michael and Isabella are sharing their story to raise awareness about brain cancer and offer hope to other families facing similar challenges.

They recently participated in a fireside chat in New York City hosted by Real Chemistry and SMAC, where they discussed their family’s experience navigating Isabella’s diagnosis, mental health, caregiving, and the impact of sharing their story.

Throughout her treatment, Isabella also documented her experience through a series of YouTube vlogs and the ABC primetime documentary, “Life Interrupted: Isabella Strahan’s Fight to Beat Cancer.”

For Michael, helping others is a value he learned from his parents. He recalled how his father used his transportation business in Germany to support people in need after retiring from the military.

“[He] would take donations, and use his money and his trucks, and drive stuff to Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, and drop it off there at local churches and the shelters for people, who he had no connection with,” said Michael. “So for me, I think I do what I feel is on my heart and what’s important to me.”

For parents caring for children with cancer, Michael emphasized that it’s OK to feel overwhelmed or emotional. He encouraged them to show their children love and support while helping them maintain hope for the future.

“I think positivity is the main thing because it was so tough on her at the time when she was [saying], ‘I can’t do it. I can’t do this. I can’t do that,’” said Michael.

Michael said he made a conscious effort to replace words like “can’t” and “if” with “when” while encouraging Isabella during treatment.

“Anytime she got down on herself, I’d say, ‘when you go back to college, when you do this, when you do that,’” said Michael. “And I just think the positive attitude and the love that you can give and the confidence that you can display towards your loved one [or] your child who’s going through something like this is the only thing you can do because you’re at the mercy of medicine.”

Now in her senior year at USC, Isabella is looking ahead to life after graduation.

“[There’s] a lot of interesting opportunities and things that I want to pursue,” she said.

Michael has no doubt she will find her way.

“She’s so talented, and this experience, in my opinion, has opened up my eyes to more talent that she has that I didn’t realize…the talent to connect people, and be in front of a crowd. I always thought she’d be nervous because I get nervous, but she’s better than me,” he said.

#4875. The 17 Most Beautiful Ski Resorts to Visit This Winter—Including Three in the US

When winter arrives, the world’s most idyllic mountain towns transform into playgrounds for serious adrenaline seekers. But, as the most beautiful ski resorts prove, the appeal of an extraordinary alpine escape extends well beyond its slopes. Why kick off your ski boots just anywhere when you could do so in a castle-like hotel in the Swiss Alps or a secluded Japanese ryokan tucked among snow-covered forests? Sure, the world-renowned runs are worth traveling for, but sometimes so are the ski hotels themselves. Think Michelin-starred restaurants, award-winning spas, art-filled interiors, and architecture that makes the most of its dramatic surroundings. Here, AD rounds up 17 of the most beautiful ski resorts to visit this winter, whether you’re an alpine ace, a beginner ski bum, or purely an après enthusiast.

Getting to Zaborin Ryokan is an adventure in itself, which means you know it’ll be good. After landing at New Chitose Airport in Sapporo, it’s a two-hour drive to the ryokan, which is hidden in the Hanazono woods of Hokkaido. Arriving at the property feels like discovering some sort of secretive lair from a Bond flick—a series of low-lying villas covered in snow suddenly reveal themselves. Built on natural hot springs, each of the villas has its own indoor and outdoor onsen, plus floor-to-ceiling windows and a private balcony with views of Mount Yōtei, the area’s dormant volcano, in the distance. Make an appointment with the in-house matcha master and prepare your taste buds for a multicourse Japanese kaiseki meal. If you can tear yourself away from your absurdly serene suite long enough to ski or snowboard, the ryokan will arrange your transfer to and from Hanazono Niseko ski area, just seven minutes away by car.

Modernist design meets mountainside adventure at Pendry Park City, a ski-in, ski-out luxury resort where “hitting the slopes” means basically just stepping outside. Tucked in Canyons Village at Park City Mountain—the largest ski resort in the US, with over 7,000 skiable acres spread across two connected mountains—this slopeside sanctuary is right next to the brand-new, high-speed Sunrise Gondola. After a day appreciating the powder, guests gather at Après Pendry for fondue and crème brulée espresso martinis either by the fire or outside. Alternatively, they head up to the rooftop for a dip in the year-round heated pool and hot tub, plus immaculate mountain views.

Located in St. Moritz, Switzerland, the Carlton Hotel boasts 60 luxurious suites that blend old-world grandeur with contemporary elements. The resort is also home to the Michelin-starred restaurant Da Vittorio.

The Gstaad Palace in Switzerland opened in 1913 and has catered to jet-setters and stars such as Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly, and Marlene Dietrich throughout its long history. The castlelike hotel overlooks the streets of Gstaad, which are filled with high-end boutiques.

The Pines Lodge, a RockResort is a rustic Colorado retreat with ski-in, ski-out access set above Beaver Creek Village. After a long day on the slopes, guests can enjoy views of the Rockies from the acclaimed Grouse Mountain Grill.

Architect Mario Botta designed the striking spa at the Tschuggen Grand Hotel in Arosa, Switzerland. The alpine retreat, which was built in 1929, features 130 rooms and suites with opulent interiors by Carlo Rampazzi.

Designed by architect Sybille de Margerie, the intimate Cheval Blanc Courchevel in Courchevel, France, is the ultimate in alpine luxury. The resort, which is owned by LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, is also filled with blue-chip artwork by Michel Othoniel, Xavier Veillant, and Bruno Peinado, whose Trojan Horse sculpture is seen here.

Founded by railway tycoon William Cornelius Van Horne in 1888, the Fairmont Banff Springs is set within Banff National Park and offers stunning views of the Canadian Rockies. The sprawling hotel, which was inspired by a Scottish baronial castle, includes 764 rooms and suites and nine restaurants and bars.

The St. Regis Aspen Resort in the Colorado Rockies received a $40 million makeover by interior architect Lauren Rottet in 2012. Set at the base of Aspen Mountain, the hotel includes 179 rooms and suites outfitted with Ralph Lauren beds and desks and marble-lined baths.

The ski-in, ski-out Hôtel des Dromonts in Avoriaz, France, was built in the 1960s by architect Jacques Labro, who was inspired by the work of Le Corbusier and Charlotte Perriand. The interiors of the distinctive angular building were recently refreshed and upgraded by designer Jocelyne Sibuet.

Munich-based firm Oikios Architect took inspiration from pine cones for the design of the InterContinental Davos in Davos, Switzerland. The oval façade uses over 790 curved, overlapping steel panels to create the scaled appearance. Inside, 216 tasteful guest rooms overlook the city—home to the World Economic Forum—and surrounding mountains.

Offering a unique combination of Asian-inspired design motifs and alpine rustic touches, The Chedi Andermatt is one of Switzerland’s most wonderful offerings. The boutique hotel is located 4,747 feet above sea level and includes a 25,833-square-foot spa to take advantage of when you’re not out on the slopes.

With rustic and understated architecture and interiors, Le Chalet Zanier is designed to mimic the natural beauty of the surrounding Mont Blanc mountain range. The resort is made up of a 12-room main structure as well as a separate three-bedroom private cottage. Like the snowflakes that top the roofs, no room is exactly like any of the others.

Located in a densely wooded area, Forestis is situated exactly where the Austrian monarchy established a tuberculosis sanatorium in 1912. Designed with simplicity in mind, the rich stone, wood, and glass of the hotel are inspired by the nature that surrounds it.

#4874. This Popular Supplement May Also Be the Key Behind Healthier Knees

You’re probably not getting enough of it, either.

Knee osteoarthritis can be a debilitating condition due to the joint pain, stiffness, and swelling it causes. Unfortunately, it's a reality for an estimated 14 million Americans. There are a range of potential treatment options that can help, including cortisone shots and GLP-1s, but a new study suggests a more accessible option may also help: taking a fiber supplement.

Research from a recent clinical trial published in the journal Nutrients suggests that adding a daily fiber supplement could ease pain from knee osteoarthritis, strengthen your muscles, and maybe even make you feel pain less intensely.

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recommends having 14 grams of fiber for every 1,000 calories you consume, which means most women should aim for 25 grams of fiber daily, while men should strive for 38 grams each day. But the average American only eats around 17 grams of fiber per day, suggesting that many of us consistently fall short on this important nutrient.

Experts aren’t saying that you should take a fiber supplement instead of physical therapy or seeing a specialist for knee pain. But if you're doing everything else right, adding a fiber supplement to your routine might be worth trying out. Here's why.

Meet the experts: Afroditi Kouraki, lead study author and researcher in the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham; Will Harvey, MD, rheumatologist at Tufts Medical Center and president of the American College of Rheumatology; Timothy Gibson, MD, orthopedic surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Joint Replacement Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California

For the study, researchers recruited 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis and split them into four groups. One group took a 20-gram daily inulin supplement (inulin is a naturally occurring fiber that's considered a prebiotic—it’s also commonly found in healthier soda alternatives), another did digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE), the third group did a combination of inulin and physical therapy, and the final group took a placebo.

Researchers discovered that people in the inulin and PT groups had less knee pain, and that people who took inulin had other perks that didn't surface in the physical therapy group, like better grip strength and less pain sensitivity. Also worth noting: Those who took inulin were more likely to stick with their prescribed treatment compared to the 21 percent of people in the PT-only group who dropped out.

“Earlier studies had linked certain gut bacteria, such as Streptococcus, to worse knee pain,” says Afroditi Kouraki, lead study author and researcher at the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham. That, plus feedback from people suffering from knee arthritis who said they wanted diet-based ways to manage their pain, led Kouraki and her team to study inulin.

The researchers didn't study the why behind this association, but experts have a few theories. "Good gut bacteria feed on fiber like inulin and, in doing so, they produce substances that calm inflammation and help keep the gut lining healthy," Kouraki says. Your gut "talks" to your brain and nerves, and it can influence how sensitive you are to pain, she explains.

Kouraki points out that people in the study who took inulin also had higher levels of the gut hormone GLP-1 (yep, that GLP-1), which is also tied to pain regulation, and that those with bigger rises in GLP-1 tended to have a stronger grip. "These clues are early, and we need more research to understand exactly what’s going on," she says.

But it's important to put the findings into context. "Exercise still did more to improve walking and chair-rise ability, which matters for patients," says Timothy Gibson, MD, orthopedic surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Joint Replacement Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

And while the findings suggested perks with taking an inulin supplement, they weren't huge differences, points out Will Harvey, MD, rheumatologist at Tufts Medical Center and president of the American College of Rheumatology. "At best, further study is warranted," he says.

People concerned about their joints will often take collagen, glucosamine and/or chondroitin. But "there is no strong evidence to support the use of dietary supplements," Dr. Harvey says.

Kouraki also points out that collagen and glucosamine are aimed at the joint itself, while inulin works indirectly through the gut bacteria and the body’s immune and hormone systems. "It’s a different approach, using diet and the gut to help manage symptoms,” she says.

Knee pain is complicated, and it's a stretch to say that taking a fiber supplement will make everything better. "This doesn’t replace proven treatments like exercise and physiotherapy, which also worked well in our study," Kouraki says. "But it suggests diet could be a useful extra tool."

And, of course, if you're in pain and it's not getting better, talk to your doctor. They should be able to suggest alternative strategies to make you more comfortable.

#4872. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.

#4868. Not Ready For a Facelift? No Problem: Welcome to The Era of “In-Between” Treatments.

No surgery, minimal downtime, a firmer, more lifted look—what’s not to love?

THE RISE OF BUZZY noninvasive in-office treatments is no coincidence. These days, people want to look sculpted, lifted, and more refreshed without having to make the somewhat uneasy decision to go under the knife. And as more and more patients seek meaningful results without committing to surgery, there’s a growing interest in treatments that bridge the gap between injectables and a facelift, aptly dubbed the “in-between” treatments.

These interventions will still give you meaningful lifting, volumizing, sculpting, and tightening results without as much downtime (sometimes, none at all) or diminishing returns on your investment. Think of them as the individualized, targeted treatments you can utilize before considering a face or neck lift. The trick is having a solid understanding of what specific technologies can—and cannot—accomplish. If you’re not pairing the right treatment with the right concern, you’re shelling out good money to “correct something it fundamentally cannot address,” explains Connie Yang, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City.

Filler, for instance, is effective for restoring strategic areas of volume loss on the face, but it can’t truly lift tissue or remove excess skin. “If you add more filler in an attempt to recreate a sharper jawline or lift the lower face, you’re just going to end up making the face look heavier and puffier, rather than more lifted and sculpted,” says Dr. Yang.

Meet the experts: Connie Yang, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. Jennifer Levine, MD, is a double board-certified facial plastic surgeon in New York City.

In a similar vein to filler, energy-based skin devices such as radio frequency (think: Morpheus 8 or Xerf) or ultrasound devices such as Ultherapy that target the deeper, structural layers of the face can only do so much up to a certain point. “These treatments can give meaningful improvement in the right patient, but there’s a limit to how much contraction you can achieve non-surgically,” says Dr. Yang. If someone has significant jowling, excess skin, or deeper tissue descent, repeated treatment with these types of devices will end up giving someone only progressively smaller improvements over time.

To give you the LD on all of your options, we spoke with experts about what each treatment can realistically accomplish, what patients can expect over time results-wise, and when you should skip straight to surgery.

As a rule of thumb, most (not all) aesthetic professionals will generally advise you to exhaust all options before spending a pretty penny on a facelift. In the end, it’s an individual decision. Either way, in-office treatments can help to keep your skin radiant and build collagen to help you to get an even better result for when it is time for a facelift. Think about throwing a crumpled up sheet over your mattress in the morning: If you don’t iron it first, the wrinkles will still be there when you go to make the bed.

There's no one-size-fits-all approach because not all facial aging is the same. For patients that are truly getting closer to being surgical candidates, “focusing on improving skin quality and some degree of skin tightening can be your best bet, while at the same time managing expectations of the limitations of devices and their expected outcomes,” says Dr. Yang.

Double board-certified facial plastic surgeon Jennifer Levine, MD, who uses a combination of injectable treatments and non-surgical devices in addition to surgery in her practice, recommends treatment protocols depending on which components of aging are most responsible for the patient’s concerns.

The following treatment categories are considered the in-betweeners that you may want to consider before going under the knife.

“This is an important option for select patients with earlier skin laxity who want gradual tightening and a degree of lifting,” says Dr. Levine. Ultrasound imaging allows providers to actually visualize tissue layers and guide energy placement.

It’s FDA-cleared for use to lift the brows and help with lax tissue beneath the chin and neck—the places where aging skin can be most obvious. “I consider it an in-between treatment because it can address laxity through targeted tissue remodeling while the patient’s expectations remain appropriate for a nonsurgical result,” says Dr. Yang, but “[they do] not replicate the degree of lifting you can achieve surgically.”

These work best when texture, dermal remodeling, and modest tightening are the goals. Dr. Levine says that for these treatments, energy settings and treatment depth play a huge role and must be chosen carefully based on anatomy. RF microneedling is provider-dependent, especially because at the wrong setting, facial fat loss, unintended scarring, and nerve injury can occur.

“I consider this particularly valuable when fine lines, uneven pigmentation, and textural changes contribute substantially to an aged appearance,” explains Dr. Levine. Improving the skin’s surface can make a meaningful aesthetic difference, especially for someone who is beginning to develop skin laxity. She points out that “improvement in skin quality is a different endpoint from repositioning descended facial tissue.”

Ellacor is the best example of a true in-between option, says Dr. Yang, “because it actually removes microscopic cores of skin without surgery, allowing the skin to contract as it heals.” Instead of just heating the skin to stimulate collagen, it uses tiny hollow needles to physically remove microscopic columns of excess skin, scarlessly. As the skin heals, it contracts and remodels, which can help to improve wrinkles and laxity.

Patient selection for this treatment is especially important because there is some downtime involved and a risk of pigment change. That said, it’s useful for those with mild to moderate laxity and early jowling, who don’t quite have enough excess skin or tissue to warrant a facelift yet.

Brand Names: Sculptra, Radiesse, Juvederm, Restylane

When true volume deficiency contributes to someone’s overall concern, Dr. Levine says that conservative volume restoration with the use of hyaluronic acid fillers or biostimulatory injectables that boost skin’s own collagen production can help to improve contours and balance the face.

Let’s just get this out of the way right off the bat—age alone isn’t the biggest determining factor in whether or not someone would benefit from a facelift. Genetics, lifestyle choices, and how someone cares for their body and skin have a huge impact. “I have patients in their 40s with very little laxity who are excellent candidates for non-invasive treatments and younger patients whose anatomy or degree of tissue descent make certain treatments less effective,” explains Yang.

And while there’s no single telltale sign to know when it’s time for a facelift, one of the main factors is whether the patient has “skin laxity alone or true tissue descent that requires surgical repositioning,” says Dr. Yang. With skin laxity, the skin can appear creepy or loose with decreased elasticity and can be pinched more easily. “Tissue descent is a deeper structural change; if you manually reposition the deeper tissue upward and it significantly restores the contours of the cheek or jawline, that tells me that the concern isn’t just loose skin and that a facelift would be the solution,” explains Dr. Yang.

Even if someone is a candidate for a non-invasive treatment, if they're ultimately looking for a dramatic lift or significant change in their facial contours, then surgery may be the answer. Dr. Yang says that she is more inclined to recommend surgery after a patient has gone through multiple rounds of injectables or tightening treatments and they continue to chase the same concern with diminishing improvement or returns. “At that point, continuing to add filler or repeatedly treating with devices can become costly without addressing the underlying structural issue,” she says.

Before diving face first into a surgery, Dr. Yang encourages her own patients to really explore all of their options and think deeply about their long-term goals. If you know that a facelift is in your future, it may shape what is recommended to you by a provider. “I don’t want you spending years of over-treating or investing in procedures that may only give you marginal improvement.” Instead, she says, the focus should be on maintaining skin quality and aging well until you’re ready. Conversely, if you’re unsure whether surgery will ever be an option for you, finding the right provider to work with can help you to maximize non-surgical options available in order to get the most meaningful results possible.

Overall, the goal should be to maximize what you have and age well, while recognizing when you’ve reached the limitations of non-surgical treatments. “If surgery may eventually be the right choice, you want to arrive there with healthy, well-maintained skin,” she says. Amen to that.
