#4833. How to Live a Life You Would Never Have Chosen

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Twenty years ago, I was diagnosed with a form of autoimmune arthritis. I’d had symptoms since college, but I had never been properly diagnosed. Two of my three brothers suffer from a form of the same disease. By the time of my diagnosis, it had seeped into every aspect of my life.

Up until then I was able to make accommodations through rest, early bedtimes, and appropriate exercise. However, in my early 40s, things heated up to the point that it became difficult to work. I have now been home and disabled for 13 years. On a good day, I may feel normal for a few hours in the afternoon. But if I overdo the most banal of activity, I will pay with more fatigue and joint pain later.

This is all to say that not feeling well and all the medical complications this entails are now the main subject of my life. As a psychiatrist who was in practice for 23 years, I am very familiar with people who are in a similar boat. Most of my patients did not feel well due to mental suffering (although some physical symptoms, such as fatigue, weakness, headache, and GI upset were common).

One thing all of us had in common was that the rest of the world had little awareness of our plight. In normal life, your body strikes a simple deal: give it ample rest and nutrition, and it allows you to go through your day and attend to what needs to be done without making a fuss. Other than meal and bedtime, it doesn’t bother you with demands for attention. When you are chronically ill, this is turned on its head. Your body demands attention like a fractious child. Due to its various aches and pains, it requires constant adjustments in your activity and mindset. Trying to feel better and dealing with how you feel is your full-time job.

Assuming, as is sadly the case, that many of these illnesses never get better, the question arises of how to live your life in the face of constant discomfort and a background of an increasing number of losses and limitations. For those of us in that situation, this is the real task of our days. The temptation and natural response is to try to feel better and imagine a better day just around the corner. But this makes you a hamster on a wheel.

What then is the path? Surely, we cannot give up some hope of improvement and attempts to stay healthy and, just perhaps, find a way forward. No, don’t give this up. Keep it on the back burner. But there is more work to be done.

The two central tasks of chronic illness are acceptance and a way to find meaning in a life you would never have chosen.

But don’t acceptance and hope contradict one another? How can we accept our losses, limitations and feeling poorly each day while we work and hope to improve our lot? The way to accomplish this is to remain aware that you are treading two paths. Yes, you must go to the doctor. Do your exercises and get a great deal of rest. You must avoid taxing situations and stay home a great deal of the time. Here, in fact, is where acceptance begins. It is exactly in living your life in ways that you would not choose where you seek to open yourself and accept your situation without a mental struggle. Letting go of this struggle does not mean letting go of hope for some change.

Acceptance includes a frank and often painful acknowledgment of where you are and what is lost to you. But in the long run, the pain of reliving your losses over and over is alleviated by acceptance. You must do your best to remain as healthy as possible while simultaneously acknowledging your limitations.

Part of this is a mourning process no different than the loss of a loved one. There is anger, bargaining, sadness, and hopefully acceptance. No more struggling with what might have been. This is harder for the chronically sick as the losses continue and some of these feelings will be revisited. That is part of the work.

When I first stopped working, I wondered how much more of myself could I lose and still feel like me. It turns out that I can lose a great deal and still be me. I have always understood myself as the sum of what I’ve accomplished in even one day. That obviously no longer works. You come to realize that despite your losses you remain yourself in the most fundamental of ways. How you treat people, what you value, and where you spend your limited attention continue to define you.

What I have found to be a more difficult question is finding meaning in your new existence. This is unfortunately an exercise that is not based on an equal distribution of luck in life. Those with more resources, more connections, and just plainly more opportunities have more chances of finding how to live a meaningful life. Here, as with anything else, you must play the cards you are dealt.

Meaning is based on values and will develop from what we find important. Interest and the involvement of other people are good places to start. But if you are stuck at home and cannot reliably get out to meetings, especially in the evening, how is this done? Unfortunately, there is no formula. Use of the Internet is a modern godsend to people like us. It makes possible connections to groups and causes that would otherwise be inaccessible. In addition, there are ways to learn new things, new skills, hobbies, etc.

There are times when this has felt to me like make-work. Usually, I have reverted to writing about psychiatry and illness, the two things I know and care about. But people vary a great deal in these personal matters. You do not need to start a charity, write a book, or learn a foreign language. Creativity, connecting to others, or just learning something new may bring new meaning to your days.

As I write this, though, it feels unsatisfactory. Recommending hobbies on YouTube does not truly feel like a way to find meaning, but rather more of a pastime. The very best suggestions I have given are not meaningful in and of themselves. Rather, they are pathways into your own deeper sense of importance and interest. This becomes a highly personal matter that only you can judge.

However personal and unique to you, it is an important part of your path through life with chronic illness. The journey is no longer through the outside world—as illness takes much of that away—but into yourself. The various pastimes are doorways into your internal life. This is where you now spend most of your time and where you must plant a flag to declare the continued importance of your very existence.

#4832. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a new study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

They said their findings are important because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

The participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

However, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”

Shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi said genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”

#4830. You’re Making Big Decisions for a Person You’ve Never Met

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

The life I had at 22, along with the one I pictured ahead of me, no longer exists.

I was living in New York City, auditioning weekly for commercial dance roles and cruise-line troupes while pursuing my degree in creative writing. I’d spent years learning how to pick up choreography in 15 minutes and write a poem that holds a feeling it never names. If you had told that person she would end up doing neuropsychological evaluations in a Boston hospital, she would not have believed you, because she could not have pictured it.

She knew who she was at that time, but she was simultaneously wrong about what her future would look like.

Psychologists have a name for this failure of vision: the end-of-history illusion. It's the tendency to recognize how much you have changed while predicting that the changing is now largely over. In six studies with more than 19,000 people aged 18 to 68, participants at every age reported substantial change over the previous decade and yet forecast far less for the decade ahead. A 30-year-old looks back at 20 and sees a different person. She looks forward to 40 and sees her present self, slightly adjusted.

The pattern held for personality traits, core values, and everyday preferences. It held for the 18-year-olds and for the 68-year-olds. Everyone, apparently, believes they have just now arrived at the finished version.

The lease is 30 years long, and you are signing it on behalf of someone you have never met. That is the practical problem, as the decisions that bind hardest tend to cluster in your late twenties and thirties: the mortgage, the specialty, the city, the degree, the name, the person. You make them with full information about your current preferences and almost no imagination for your future ones.

The more unsettling finding is who we think we are predicting for.

Emily Pronin and Lee Ross found that when people describe their future selves, they reach for the same explanatory style they use for strangers. We explain our current behavior by pointing to circumstances: the week was brutal, the request was unreasonable. We explain other people’s behavior by pointing to their character. And we explain our future selves’ behavior the way we explain others: from the outside.

A 2024 study found the end-of-history pattern in children as young as four, across two experiments with 256 participants, including a design in which the same child was asked about both past and future. A third experiment asked children about other people. In that study, the illusion disappeared. Children can imagine that someone else will change, but can’t see their own change coming.

What we learned from this study is that the future version of you gets handled by the part of your mind that imagines people you have not met.

There is a whole literature on closing the gap, built around what researchers call future self-continuity, or how connected you feel to the person you will become. The interventions are inventive: writing a letter to yourself 20 years out, viewing an age-progressed photograph. More recently, a team at MIT built a system that lets you hold a conversation with an AI-generated version of yourself at 60; in a preregistered study of 344 young adults, a single session lowered reported anxiety and raised a sense of connection to the future self.

However, in late 2025, a team went looking for studies that had tested these techniques. They screened more than 1,200 papers and found 14. Fewer than half of those bothered to check whether the exercise had actually changed how connected participants felt to their future selves, which was the whole premise. And nearly all the participants were college students in their twenties. Not one study asked whether this works differently at 40.

In other words, the technique that makes you feel closer to your future self has not been shown to make you better at predicting it.

I don’t think you need to successfully forecast the person you will be in 2036, and the research gives no reason to think you could.

The goal is to have humility about the forecast you are making. When you make a decision that binds, beyond choosing between options, you’re making a prediction that the person living with the consequences will want what you want today. The research has shown that prediction is almost certainly too confident.

Decisions differ in what they cost if you change. A lease and a mortgage both bind you, but one releases you in a year. A degree and a license both take years, but only one of them travels. That difference is a property of the decision rather than of the person making it.

So extend some grace backward. The decisions you now find baffling were made by someone operating with the same blind spot you have right now, and they were doing their best with a self they could not see past.

My creative-writing major self was not wrong. She just could not have known that learning to read a line for what it does not say would turn out to be useful in a room where someone is describing their memory loss and leaving out the part that frightens them.

Ersner-Hershfield, H., Wimmer, G. E., & Knutson, B. (2009). Saving for the future self: Neural measures of future self-continuity predict temporal discounting. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 4(1), 85–92. doi.org/10.1093/scan/nsn042

Harris, H., & Busseri, M. A. (2019). Is there an ‘end of history illusion’ for life satisfaction? Evidence from a three-wave longitudinal study. Journal of Research in Personality, 83, 103869. doi.org/10.1016/j.jrp.2019.103869

Hershfield, H. E., Brimhall, C. I., & Kerbel, S. (2025). Exploring the distribution and correlates of future self-continuity in a large, nationally representative sample. Judgment and Decision Making, 20, e9. doi.org/10.1017/jdm.2024.23

#4829. The 10 Best Face Washes for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Soaps from Kiehl’s and Tower 28 came out on top in our testing.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

EVERY GOOD SKINCARE routine starts with the same thing—a quality face wash. Before you layer on serums, moisturizers, and eye creams, you need to clear the canvas. A face wash does exactly that by clearing away dirt and grime that accumulate on your skin while also helping prevent clogged pores that can trigger breakouts. That’s why it’s crucial to find the best face wash for you, no matter your skin type.

Wash your face every morning, night, and after heavy workouts to remove bacteria and sebum before they build up, says dermatologistDr. Anthony Rossi, MD. The best face washes for men go beyond cleaning: they hydrate, fight acne, and control excess oil. This first step in your routine is especially important if you live an active lifestyle. While cardio workouts boost circulation and support collagen production, sweat can leave your skin vulnerable to breakouts and irritation.

With so many products out there, finding the right one for your skin type and preferences can feel impossible. That’s why I spent the last two years testing every cleanser I could get my hands on to find the ten best face washes for virtually any skin type and price point.

A face wash is the cornerstone of any skincare routine—without it, the rest of your products won’t work as well. Choose one that’s gentle yet effective because even if your entire routine is just washing your face, you don’t want a cleanser that strips away your skin’s natural oils.

Matching your face wash to your skin type ensures it works with your skin’s natural needs, clears and balances your complexion, and primes your face for the products that follow.

We’ve been testing face washes and cleansers since this story was first published in 2021. As Men's Health's Grooming Editor, I’m also constantly trying out the latest releases to determine which are worth adding to your rotation. For this update, I considered picks from previous iterations of this roundup, as well as current favorites from fellow Men's Health writers and editors. This ultimately led to me testing over 50 face washes, evaluating their ingredients, feel, consistency, and effectiveness. Below is the culmination of this extensive hands-on research: the ten best face washes for men with any skin type or budget.

For active guys who want a no-nonsense soap that still feels luxurious, this cleanser from Kiehl's delivers. Formulated with hydrating glycerin and squalane—and free of parabens and fragrances—it thoroughly cleanses without stripping moisture. Its powerful ingredients clean and hydrate at the same time, leaving your skin soft, balanced, and primed for the rest of your routine.

Testing Notes: I’ve used Kiehl's cleanser for years and love its ultra-smooth formula that glides easily over my skin. I appreciate that it’s fragrance-free, making it ideal for sensitive skin. Lightweight, gentle, moisturizing, and nourishing, it’s one of the most versatile cleansers I’ve tried—perfect for any skin type. At $16 for 2.5 oz, it isn’t the cheapest option, but it’s still on the affordable side of the market. Because it foams so well, I only need a small amount for a full wash, and one container lasts me about two months with daily use. Overall, Kiehl's Ultra Facial Cleanser remains my go-to everyday face wash, no matter your skin type or budget.

This gel cleanser uses zinc, copper, and magnesium to support the skin’s natural defenses while boosting hydration. Aloe vera then locks in moisture and forms a soothing barrier, while oat calms irritation and comforts sensitive skin. Fragrance-free, it gently removes makeup, sunscreen, and daily buildup without stripping or irritating—even for the most reactive skin.

Testing Notes: I don’t have rosacea, but my skin is prone to redness, so I was excited to see this cleanser approved by the National Rosacea Society—and it didn’t disappoint. Whenever my skin flares up, I use it daily, and within a week or two (depending on severity), the redness quickly calms. Its silky consistency also leaves my skin feeling smooth, balanced, and healthy.

You can’t go wrong with a classic. This Cetaphil cleanser, formulated for combination to oily, sensitive skin, actively removes dirt and excess oil while protecting your skin’s natural barrier. The blend of B vitamins and glycerin nourishes as it cleanses, leaving your face refreshed, balanced, and never tight or dry.

Testing Notes: Cetaphil’s Daily Facial Cleanser delivers incredible value for its price. I love that it packs the same hero ingredients you’d see in pricier formulas, like glycerin and niacinamide, yet it’s gentle enough for even ultra-sensitive skin. It leaves my face feeling clean but never stripped, which makes it easy to reach for every day. My only gripe? I wish the pump dispenser worked more smoothly—it can be frustrating when I’m half-asleep and just want a quick wash.

Long before CeraVe went viral on TikTok, grooming experts swore by the drugstore brand for its high-quality ingredients at budget-friendly prices. A perfect example is this cleanser, packed with hydrating staples like hyaluronic acid and ceramides that strengthen the skin barrier while keeping moisture locked in.

Testing Notes: CeraVe’s Facial Cleanser is one of my go-to budget face washes because it’s easy to find online or in stores, and it simply works. I’ve been using CeraVe since my early 20s, and I can honestly say the formula has never let me down—it removes excess oil and grime without ever causing breakouts.

Shaped like a deodorant stick but designed for your face, this solid soap from Oars and Alps packs charcoal, a buzzy exfoliant that gently scrubs without irritation. I love that even a 1.4-oz container lasts over a month when used daily.

Testing Notes: Oars and Alps’ cleansing stick has become my go-to TSA-friendly face soap for traveling and camping. I love how portable it is and how easily it applies—just like my favorite deodorant—while still exfoliating and removing dirt. It easily fits in my Dopp kit, and I don’t need to worry about it leaking or opening. Plus, my face feels incredibly clean after each use, and a little product really does go a long way.

Finding a TSA-friendly cleanser that doesn't spill is hard. That's where Jaxon Lane's Shake and Wake comes in. It's a powder-to-cream product that gently exfoliates skin and cleans just as well as a liquid cleanser, thanks to a powerful combo of niacinamide, vitamin E, and vitamin C. In other words, it's a Dopp kit must-have.

Testing Notes: The first thing I noticed about this wash was its powdery consistency. What surprised me was how much I liked it—and how often I keep reaching for it, especially when traveling. Similar to Oars and Alps Solid Wash, there is minimal risk of spilling—and even if it did (which I’ve yet to experience), the powder will be far less destructive than liquid.

It feels ultra-gentle on my skin and transforms into a soap-like lather as soon as it hits water. The container is TSA-friendly, tightly sealed, and unlikely to leak, and since it’s powder, even a spill would be minimal and far less messy than a gel.

If you're somebody who loves the smell of the great outdoors, or that irreplaceable feeling felt (and smelt) the early morning after a night of camping, then this face wash is for you. Loaded with skin-boosting natural ingredients like aloe vera, caffeine, and charcoal, Dr. Squatch's face wash exfoliates, refreshes, and cleanses with the best of them.

Testing Notes: With its unique charcoal-backed texture and feel, this wash is one of the most rejuvenating options out there. But what really stands out is its understated, yet still attention-grabbing pine tar scent—subtle enough to avoid clashing with your cologne, but woodsy enough to raise the nostrils in the best way possible.

For those with sensitive or dry skin, there are few (if any) better skincare brands than La Roche-Posay. And the brand's cleanser is a perfect representation of why. Its niacinamide-backed formula is equally gentle and hydrating. Add in other moisturizing winners like glycerin, along with the lack of any skin-aggravating ingredients like heavy fragrances or sulfates, and you have one of the lowest risk, highest reward face washes on the market.

Testing Notes: I have sensitive skin and love this cleanser because it never irritates me. Even if your skin is less reactive, the creamy lather feels amazing during and after each wash. It’s gentle and leaves skin feeling hydrated and healthy.

Talk about value—at under $7 a container, it’s hard to find a more effective, affordable face wash for men than Harry’s. Best known for its stellar shave gear, the brand has quietly expanded into no-nonsense men’s skincare, including standouts like its facial moisturizer. This face wash follows the same formula: it packs low-key hydrators like eucalyptus and peppermint alongside gentle exfoliants like glycerin, delivering a no-BS cleanse that gets the job done without breaking the bank.

Testing Notes: Harry’s hasn’t strayed from its facial-hair roots, as this cleanser doubles as one of the best beard washes, softening whiskers and priming them for trimming or shaving. I also can’t overstate how foamy it gets; it not only strips away dirt and buildup but also makes each (already affordable) container last a long time.

Anyone who struggles with acne knows it takes over your routine, demanding protective, non-invasive, blemish-correcting products at every step. For that crucial first cleanse, Geologie’s new Acne Control Face Wash stands out as the best option. Even though it’s been on the market for barely a year, it has already become a staple for me whenever I’m facing a breakout, thanks to its 2 percent salicylic acid formula and silky-smooth application.

Testing Notes: I still reach for this wash whenever I feel a blemish or breakout coming on. The only drawback is that the gel feels a little stringy at first and needs plenty of water before it foams. Once it does, though, the lather expands quickly, and a dime-sized drop covers my entire face—making each bottle last for months.

Wash your face twice a day—morning and night. Just as important, pay attention to the products you use, avoiding harsh chemicals like sulfates and parabens. Choose a gentle cleanser for everyday use and keep an exfoliating scrub for two or three times a week. Apply the scrub with light pressure—fast, hard, and rough isn’t the answer. Overdoing it can damage your skin and create new problems. And always remember: everyone’s skin type is different. What works for one person might not work for another.

#4828. Attention All Humans: AI Is Like a Spy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Do you remember when it would take a minute or two for a website to fully load? The picture would reveal itself in incremental pixels until you could finally view it in its entirety. It was the era of banner ads and pop-ups, a rudimentary transference of billboard marketing to the World Wide Web.

Later, algorithms scanned, then shaped, our behavioral and consumption patterns. The length of time a user watched a video or stopped scrolling to “read more” became the metric for advertising effectiveness. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technology measures how you behave online, like a little spy watching your every move without your noticing.

Welcome to the attention economy. “Pay attention!” the internet demands. “Or at least get paid for it,” advertising executives suggest. That is what influencer marketing is all about. The more clicks, the more views, the more money flows.

Joe Marchese and Jonathan Bing have penned a new book, Human Dot AI, that chronicles the rise of advertising from the era of Mad Men advertisers on Madison Avenue to today. Both authors have extensive experience in the industry themselves. Marchese is an entrepreneur and media executive, CEO of Human Ventures Holdings, co-founder of Casa Komos Brands Group, and chairman of Groundswell. He previously founded true[X] and led advertising revenue at Fox Networks Group. Bing is a marketing and communications executive who has held leadership roles at Netflix, 21st Century Fox, and Vice. He is also a journalist who has written for The New York Times, Los Angeles Times, and Wired. The authors wish to help readers reclaim their attention or, in their words, to “restore a sense of agency, choice, and control over the time and attention that algorithms are not designed to give you.”

Do you remember the ads “Have a Coke and a smile” or “I’d like to teach the world to sing in perfect harmony”? They lent viewers a sense of community and connection through catchy slogans and jingles that captured our collective imagination. Watching television, in a sense, was a shared experience. No fast-forwarding through commercials, no pre-recording to watch your favorite show at a later time. The Super Bowl remains an exception as one of the most popular live televised sports events of the year in which the legendary commercials running at roughly $10 million per 30-second slot are often as memorable as the game itself. According to Nielsen, a global leader in measuring audience behavior, however, nearly half of all TV viewers have switched to streaming services such as Netflix and YouTube. In a recent video call, Marchese admitted that consuming social media today "is like watching television," but not in the same way we used to in the pre-Internet era. Today, asynchronous viewing has made watching programs a much more isolating experience.

With 5.8 billion mobile phone users worldwide, 70 percent of the planet’s population has a robust digital communications-based lifestyle. Marchese and Bing aim to offer a way back to human connection despite our AI-saturated lives. Around the time that Facebook’s News Feed feature was launched (yes, there was a time when you actually had to actively look for people by clicking on various profiles), it stopped being a place to connect and became more a place to advertise, albeit subtly. Advertising became adjacent to social activity itself, deeply embedded in the content without our realizing it. Consumer engagement became the name of the game. No more annoying pop-up ads. Enter the gamification of social media consumption. We are no longer simply consuming information (and patiently waiting for pictures to load); we are now participating in a game designed to capture and retain our attention—all day long. As a result, two problems have emerged: the lack of editorial supervision and the machines’ lack of understanding humans. Content is no longer about bringing people together but, rather, about keeping people engaged and enraged.

“[N]o algorithm can replace what happens when people come together around something real—a shared experience, story, or glass” (Marchese & Bing, 2026). An automated, algorithm-driven life flattens intimacy, commercializes our need for connection, and monetizes our very human desire to love and be loved. How we spend our time and attention truly matters. These resources are finite, but an algorithm doesn’t care why a user is engaged with the content. It is designed to feed us more of the same.

Digital hygiene is key to maintaining a sense of equilibrium in our tech-driven lives. Attention-grabbing is as old as the advertising industry itself. From the town crier to our social media apps, brands yearn for our attention. But in the end, we, as humans, get to decide if we give it or not.

Marchese, J., & Bing, J. (2026). Human Dot AI: How the Fight for Your Attention Became the World’s Biggest Business. AMPLIFY PUBLISHING.

#4827. How One Creative Couple Found Harmony in Their 1920s Los Angeles Craftsman

Nothing about where interior designer Harrison Soll is now was part of the plan. Five years ago, he was focused on his work, and he didn’t want any distractions. But when he met Rodney Burns, a stylist and owner of the legendary Los Angeles vintage gallery, Church Boutique, it set everything on a new path. They met in the fall; by New Year’s they were a couple. “I didn’t think it was going to be a relationship,” Soll says. He credits their shared interests for bringing them together: “We always found a throughline with design.”

They now live in a 1925 craftsman house in Laurel Canyon. Soll took the lead decorating the nearly 1,400-square-foot home in a combination of his and Burns’s styles with many pieces coming from Burns’s eclectic collection of vintage art, furniture, and sculpture. Burns has worked with Lenny Kravitz as a stylist and creative collaborator for the past 15 years, and the singer says he admires what Burns and Soll have created together. “The mix of Rodney’s early- to midcentury style mixed with ethnic expression next to Harrison’s bold minimalist modern approach seamlessly blend together,” Kravitz tells AD.

The backyard of Soll’s and Burns’s Laurel Canyon home is a bricolage of funky, inherited stonework and vintage pottery.

The nail art above the fireplace has a cute backstory story: Burns and Soll had seen it at a vintage shop in Santa Monica and Burns regretted not buying it. When he went back to purchase the piece, it was marked as sold. But only because Soll had already covertly bought it as a Valentine’s Day gift for Burns.

The giant Sergio Bustamante giraffe bust in the foyer is a delicate topic. “The giraffe was one of our biggest fights in decorating this house,” Burns explains. “I was determined to have that giraffe live some place in this house because he’s just fantastic, and the scale of him, and the rarity of him.” Except, counters Soll, that the placement of the giraffe is treacherous because the front door swings right in its path. “You just have to be careful,” Soll says.

The foyer—which features a collection of masks and vintage paintings—was one of the most difficult areas to style, explains Burns. The couple was trying to be selective of what pieces to incorporate from Burns’s massive collection and at one point Burns suggested putting all of his masks in storage to save for another house down the line, or passing them onto Burns’s vintage boutique, Church. Soll dissented, saying, “No, let’s put them everywhere.”

The living room features two sofas—a Joseph D’Urso for Knoll piece reupholstered in leopard fabric and a leather De Sede Terrazza. The carpet is the Antilocarpa style from Stark. A trio of fiberglass shell art was sourced through Kelly Wearstler. The art behind the sofa is a manipulated canvas garment bag by the artist Roosevelt “Rip” Woods, the first black artist to have a solo show at the Phoenix Art Museum.

As renters, there were naturally limitations on what could be achieved. Soll got permission to retile a bathroom and install a new vanity. The doe-patterned wall-to-wall carpeting in the living room was an “ask for forgiveness” move, but his landladies ended up loving it. Burns, on the other hand, needed more convincing. “The carpet took many dinners of conversations between the two of us,” Soll says.

Soll describes himself as more of a minimalist while Burns avows, “I’m a maximalist to the umpteenth power.” The couple attempted to strike a balance while still filling the space with character. Some rooms nod to Soll’s leanings toward minimalism like an office with a midcentury desk and a 1970s tapestry and the dining room where a Sergio Bustamante table and a Chinese Art Deco rug are the main attractions.

When decorating their Laurel Canyon home, Soll and Burns had to figure out how to combine their opposing styles, with Soll being more of a minimalist and Burns being a maximalist. But, says Burns, “[Soll] has made me be able to take a pause and then also make me a little less attached to some of the things that I’ve collected  and given me an opportunity to maybe show a little bit more restraint.” In the corner, a brass Maison Jansen palm tree mingles with a Sergio Bustamante monkey.

Burns, who has been styling Lenny Kravitz for over a decade, says his approach to home design and fashion are one in the same: “Building an outfit, building a room: same thing in my opinion.”

Kravitz offers these kind words on Burns: “What I love about Rodney is that he is limitless in his concepts and always thinks outside of the box. His visual vocabulary enables him to mix a vast stew of eras and genres. He pays tribute to our ancestors and uplifts new innovators. Always soulful, expressive, and elegant.”

In the dining room, Soll placed a Sergio Bustamante table on a diagonal to make enough room for the couple’s large dog. “She’s a girthy girl,” says Soll, referring to the table, not the dog. The chairs are by Paul Evans and the Chinese Art Deco rug was sourced from Ariana Rugs. The Tom Greene chandelier was sourced from Burns’s boutique, Church.

Burns’s maximalism is on display in the living room, where a couch upholstered in leopard Scalamandré mixes with zebra-hide chairs and a sinuous De Sede sofa. (That animal print couch, Soll wants you to know, also features a block of leather upholstery: “I just think it would have been too maximalist to do a full Scalamandré sofa.”)

The living room is filled with brass sculptures (a Maison Jansen palm tree and a Sergio Bustamante monkey), bronze figures sourced from an estate sale in Arizona, and several pieces of sculptural artwork.

The bedroom mixes patterns and textures with a stainless steel bed from TTMM, Paul Evans “Cityscape” nightstands, striped bedding, and antique bronze table lamps with African mud cloth shades.

The 1970s textile art in the office is a vintage find of Burns’s that Soll loves. “I used to go to Rodney’s apartment when we first started dating, and I would be like, ‘Oh my God! Like, if we break up, I’m never gonna be able to find this tapestry,’” he says.

Soll got permission from his landladies to retile the bathroom and add a new vanity. The metal Curtis Jeré artwork comes from Burns’s collection.

The bohemian architecture of the home lends quirkiness to the design. The main bedroom isn’t a perfect square, making it seem like a stainless steel bed from TTMM is placed on a diagonal but is actually following the geometry of a very funky, angular bedroom.

The couple has taken their time tinkering and adjusting the decor, taking a considered approach to collecting and combining their belongings. Soll describes the overall vibe as having an Afrocentric theme that’s also a little bit Ralph Lauren. “Our visions have mingled,” Burns says.

Still, there is one last item the couple needs to complete the design: a blanket basket. But, says Soll, “We still haven’t found one we agree upon.”

The backyard is also home to a shed (not pictured), which functions as Burns’s closet.

#4826. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4825. Every Lululemon Shoe Ranked: I Tested Them All, and I Have Thoughts

After putting Lululemon’s full shoe lineup to the test, here’s how each pair ranked.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Lululemon set the bar high for athleisure with its buttery-soft leggings, and continues to deliver on that front. However, since it had always been primarily an athletic wear brand, it wasn’t part of the running shoe or walking shoe conversation. But that changed in 2022 when Lululemon expanded into footwear. Since then, the brand has slowly built a following in that category, too.

I originally tried a pair of Lululemon sneakers a few months ago after reading rave reviews, but quickly stopped wearing them because they felt too snug at my usual size. But I kept seeing positive feedback from other people, making me wonder if I wrote them off too soon. After all, Lululemon is known for careful construction, thoughtful tailoring, and high-quality products.

Like many other shoe brands, each of Lululemon’s sneakers is designed with a specific purpose in mind. The brand’s shoes match Lululemon's overall understated aesthetic. While there are a few bright colors here and there, you also have plenty of neutrals and muted shades to choose from. That alone makes them stand out in a sea of eyeball-searing sneakers.

To see what I was missing beyond looks, I tried each of Lululemon’s athletic shoes—BeyondFeel, Split Shift, Wildfeel, and Chargefeel 3—to see which is the best. And since it’s best to know what you’re getting into before you grab a pair just because it matches your favorite gym outfit, I get into the details about each shoe model below. I was surprised at how wide of a range the brand offers: There’s a Lululemon sneaker for just about anything. Still, one had to come out on top. These are the best Lululemon shoes, ranked, based on months of testing.

The BeyondFeel is the shoe I originally passed on before because it ran snug. So, PSA: Consider sizing up if you prefer a roomy fit or have wide feet. While Lululemon says online that these fit true to size, that wasn't the case for me. Once I went up half a size, I was hooked.

The BeyondFeel is Lululemon's max cushioned shoe, so you can think of it like a Hoka Bondi 9 or On Cloudmonster 3. It's designed for everyday use. Think: running errands, power walking, actual running—it's all comfortable in the BeyondFeel.

I noticed a difference from my daily trainers the second I slipped my feet inside. The best way to describe the feeling is like the first time I put on a pair of Align leggings. I was immediately comfortable, with no chafing, pinching, or any other issues.

This shoe has a nice, roomy toe box, giving your feet plenty of room to swell naturally as you go about your day or rack up the mileage. It also has a stable heel and good grip although, heads up: The shoes may squeak a little when you first wear them inside.

Lululemon designed the BeyondFeel differently for women vs. men, adding an extra 2 millimeters of foam at the forefoot to take some pressure off the knees and hips. I wouldn't wear the BeyondFeel for long runs, though—it doesn't have much energy return, which is that slight bouncy feeling you may get in a shoe. But I was happy to log a few miles in them here and there, along with wearing them for weight training and just running errands. Their stylish look and comfortable feel make them a good choice for nearly everyone.

The Split Shift is Lululemon's neutral everyday running shoe, which is another way of saying it's a good shoe for most runners. The first thing you'll notice is how lightweight the shoe is. At 7.8 ounces, it's not the lightest shoe ever made, but it definitely won't feel like your feet are dragging you down when you're logging higher mileage. This sneaker has an equally breezy upper, giving it an overall airy feel.

I really appreciate the springiness of these shoes. It's not so much that it feels like you're running on mini trampolines, but there's a good energy return here to help propel you forward with each step. That's definitely a noticeable change from the BeyondFeel, which has pretty much no energy return by comparison. There's a gusseted tongue that gently hugs your ankle, along with some extra padding around the ankle that prevents rubbing. The outsole doesn't feel as grippy as the BeyondFeel, but it's a good choice for everyday road running.

My only complaint with the Split Shift is that the toe box runs a little narrow. I'm used to running in shoes with a wide toe box, and the Split Shift's smaller width across the toes means they probably won't be my go-to for everyday miles. Like the BeyondFeel, I'd suggest going up a half size if you like a roomy toe box or have wide feet.

Lululemon's Chargefeel 3 looks different from the brand's other shoes out of the box. It has an hourglass shape, with a narrow middle, more room at the toes, and an exaggerated base at the heel for stability. That shape is intentional, since this shoe is made for cross-training, hybrid, and HIIT workouts. The Chargefeel 3 is on the lighter end of weight for a gym shoe at 8 ounces, and it feels light on your feet. Still, it has everything you want in a shoe you'll be doing cross-training in, like a locked-in feeling in the heel, snug laces, and ability to handle lateral movements.

The grip on this shoe is impressive. I was able to stop cleanly while doing direction-changing indoor sprints at the gym, with no squeaking. The shoe also features a ShiftFoam midsole for a little energy return. Its not nearly as bouncy as the Split Shift, though—but you don't want that in a shoe you'll be doing hybrid workouts in anyway.

The Chargefeel 3 has a 6mm heel-to-toe drop, which may be high for those looking for a neutral strength training shoe, so it might not be ideal for lifting. It’s laser-cut mesh helps tamp down on foot sweat, along with Nulu fabric heel lining to mimic the feel of your favorite leggings.

And if you're looking for a running shoe, scroll up. This is really a gym shoe that you can do a little running in in a pinch—not something you want to do any significant mileage in. And while the Chargefeel 3 made me feel locked-in and secure during gym workouts, it's not so comfortable that I'd wear this shoe outside of exercise. If you're looking for a dedicated hybrid shoe, though, it's worth a look.

Some athletic shoe brands will slap deep lugs on a sneaker and call it a trail shoe without addressing other needs. But it's clear that Lululemon's Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There's a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you're going down. Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. That wasn't a huge deal on shorter runs, but it started to annoy me on longer runs. Like many others on this list, I'd consider going up a half size.

My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that's pretty common in a trail shoe. (It got better with time and more wear.) It's also worth noting that the Wildfeel isn't the most breathable shoe you'll find, and my socks were a little sweatier than usual because of it. None of these are dealbreakers. But it also meant the Wildfeel was my least favorite shoe in Lululemon's lineup.

To choose the best Lululemon shoes, I put each through regular testing over several months. I used each shoe on a near-daily basis for weeks, making sure to test it for the way it was designed. So, I wore the Wildfeel on trails and the Split Shift on daily training runs. During each testing session, I took notes on the shoe's fit, traction, stability, and overall comfort. From there, I ranked each shoe based on its testing results, along with how well it matched up to their intended use.

The best Lululemon shoe for running depends on the type of running you plan to do. If you’re in search of a neutral everyday trainer, the Split Shift is a good choice. It’s lightweight and slightly bouncy, giving you plenty of support and cushioning over daily miles. The BeyondFeel is another solid option. It’s highly cushioned for maximum comfort, making it a better choice for shorter runs.

The best Lululemon shoe for HIIT workouts is the Chargefeel 3. This sneaker has a unique hourglass shape to create a locked-in feel you’ll appreciate during HIIT workouts, along with a wide base for stability. The shoe’s grip is impressive, allowing you to stop quickly and change directions during indoor workouts.

Lululemon used to offer the Strongfeel shoe for strength training, but it’s been discontinued. Now, the Chargefeel 3 is the best option for many strength training workouts due to its wide base and stable platform. But as noted above, the shoe has a higher heel-to-toe drop of 6mm, so it’s not ideal for moves like deadlifts. So if lifting is your priority, you might want to consider a more neutral shoe for optimal biomechanics.

Lululemon often says online that its shoes fit true to size, but that wasn't my experience. I don't have wide feet, but I do appreciate a roomy toe box to accommodate the natural foot swelling that happens on workouts and runs. Most Lululemon shoes tend to run narrow across the toe box. If you have wide feet or just prefer more room to spread your toes, consider going up a size.

She has additional CES, CNC, BCS, and SFC certifications. She is also a level-2 certified Spinning instructor. Her work has appeared in Bicycling, Runner’s World, and other outlets, and her experience spans both editorial and hands-on work across the fitness industry. Whether she’s writing about training, health, or performance, she’s most interested in making complicated topics useful, approachable, and helpful. She is currently the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health.

#4824. Beware of Rehab Recruitment Scams

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Imagine you’ve been struggling with alcohol addiction. Every waking moment is spent either drinking or thinking about drinking. You don’t even want to drink anymore, but you just keep doing it. In a rare moment of lucidity, you decide it’s time to get help. This opportunity for help may come only once. Your life depends on getting genuine help right now.

But what if the person who answers the phone when you call is a salesperson, not a qualified admissions agent, and gets paid for every person they send to a specific program? What if the center offering the highest kickback this month provides a low quality of care or cuts you loose too soon? What if your family has spent their life savings to get you this care?

Situations like this are troublingly common. What’s behind them, and how can patients and their families avoid being scammed?

The following composite scenario lays out many of the practices involved in this kind of impersonation and the patient brokering that often follows.

A woman—we’ll call her Melissa—decides to seek help for opioid addiction. She googles a trusted treatment center in her town—we’ll call it Hometown Recovery—and dials the number that appears at the top of the page.

When an agent answers, Melissa breathes a sigh of relief. She believes she’s talking with someone at Hometown. The agent neither confirms nor denies Melissa’s assumption and asks what kind of insurance she has. If Melissa had Medicaid, that would likely be the end of the call. If she had private insurance, the agent would recommend a specific program “based on her insurance.”

But let’s say Melissa doesn’t have insurance at all. The agent offers to get insurance for her, for free. Melissa suspects something is off. She asks, “Is this Hometown Recovery?” The agent says, “We work with them. I can get you there,” and keeps asking questions. Melissa presses, and after she asks several times, the exasperated agent says, “Yes.”

Melissa accepts the offer for free insurance and is admitted to a program 600 miles away. She’s on a plane the next day and arrives just as withdrawal symptoms begin. She enters the center’s detox unit immediately.

In four days, she is thinking a little clearer. She wonders how she ended up here when she wanted to go to Hometown Recovery. She begins asking questions and ultimately says she wants to leave. Staff members respond that she needs to stay in detox for seven days because that’s what her insurance specified.

She agrees to stay, and at the end of seven days, she enters the center’s primary treatment program. She’s three weeks into residential care when the insurance company realizes her policy is fraudulent and cancels it. The profit-driven treatment center terminates her care. Melissa is far from home with no money, nowhere to go, and no way to get home.

Meanwhile, Hometown Recovery never heard from her. If Melissa has relatives back home who can help, she may be able to get there. But if—like so many people with her circumstances—she doesn’t have anyone, she is now homeless in a strange city after receiving partial treatment.

She took the brave step of asking for help, and she’s been robbed of an opportunity to heal. The call center hijacked her recovery, and this could prove fatal for Melissa.

Impersonation, in the business sense, involves one entity advertising or presenting as another. It’s often a way for unscrupulous businesses to capitalize on the good reputation of more established ones. In the treatment world, some independent or treatment-center-owned call centers buy ads using other centers’ exact names.

When Melissa googled her local treatment center, she saw an ad that read, “Hometown Recovery? Call Us Now!” But the call center she reached had purchased ads featuring “Hometown Recovery” as a keyword. This is an impersonation scam, and it’s illegal.

Perhaps worse than ad scams, some call centers impersonate free addiction helplines—someone trustworthy to talk to, confide in. And, like the search ad scammers, they recruit vulnerable people, either into the facility that operates the call center or the one paying the highest kickback. If you’re starting to feel as though these call centers are treating humans as a commodity, you’re not alone.

It’s truly appalling, but patient brokering (or body brokering) is when agencies or individuals receive kickbacks for funneling patients to specific treatment centers. So, instead of a person whose life is at stake being matched to the program that can best care for them, they’re turned over to the highest bidder.

Call centers are one patient brokering channel. But even police, people working in recovery, or those involved in meeting-based programs may receive kickbacks for recruitment. Likewise, some people who do street outreach—even very publicly on social media—are paid by treatment centers to bring in patients. Social media itself and websites disguised as general help are also common brokering channels.

Whether and how an influencer, agency, or trusted professional partners with those centers is scrutinized by a complex network of laws and regulations.

What happened to Melissa likely violated several federal laws and regulations, as well as some state statutes, depending upon jurisdiction. And as you might expect, the most meticulous impersonators and brokers will operate in places where state laws are more favorable, or enforcement is low.

Federally, FTC truth-in-advertising laws apply to impersonation, and health care fraud statutes are commonly used to prosecute brokering. Both practices are getting more attention recently at the state level as well, and brokering is now a felony in a few states, including North Carolina, Florida, and Arizona.

With sentences ranging from probation to four years at the high end, it’s clear that brokering laws don’t have the teeth that they should, which is possibly one reason prosecutors seem to prefer fraud charges. Given the danger it can place vulnerable people in, including some documented cases of overdose death following brokered placements, consequences are insufficient to say the least. Some advocates and survivors make a compelling argument that brokering is indistinguishable from human trafficking.

With brokers potentially lurking everywhere, they may feel impossible to avoid. And the last thing we want to do is make patients or their families feel wary of every encounter—not trusting the whole industry could present a major barrier to receiving deeply needed care.

There are a few simple ways to spot scammers and brokers:

Report anything suspicious to the FTC and your state attorney general. Additionally, watch for the following red flags:

When you (or a loved one) reach out for help, the person receiving that call should always treat it as the only chance to save your life. The inhumanity of recovery impersonation scamming and patient brokering is hard to comprehend, but our hope is that knowing a bit about these practices will help you find the right treatment path.
