#4774. How Dwight Howard Built His ‘Superman’ Physique

The NBA center talks training, injuries, and discipline.

MORE THAN OTHER pro athletes, NBA players tend to enter their professional careers as skinny kids, still developing out of high school. To a degree, that’s exactly what happened with Dwight Howard, the first pick of the 2004 NBA draft. “My first year in the league, I got kind of pushed around,” Howard said on MH’s Strong Talk. “I didn’t like it.” Howard spent that offseason “eating weights” and became on the most muscular (and dominant) players ever. He earned the nickname “Superman” and went on to a Hall of Fame career. For almost two decades, Howard played for multiple teams and won an NBA championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020.

Howard’s superhero physique came from more than shooting hoops. The center began building a disciplined training regimen as a high schooler, waking up at 4 a.m. to run track and hit the weight room.

“I told my dad at 10 I wanted to go to the NBA, and he said, ‘Well, you got to learn how to sacrifice now. You know your time and your effort. You have to learn how to be disciplined,’” Howard says in the latest Strong Talk episode.

Howard took his dad’s words to heart, already having the foresight that establishing a routine now would be easier than breaking bad training habits upon entering the NBA. His training over the years has evolved into different fitness challenges: from training in high-altitude terrains in Aspen to taking on Pilates and yoga.

Speaking with MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and exercise physiologist and strength coach Dr. Pat Davidson, Howard goes into detail about the strength exercises he did to stay fit during the season, what he’s learned from trying to play through injuries, and the upcoming launch of the Rize Above with Dwight app next month that will offer fitness guidance to individuals of any age starting a fitness journey.

#4773. Journaling Can Get Anxiety Out of Your Head

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Sometimes the mind won’t stop looping and replaying. Anxiety has a way of showing up at the most inconvenient times. You're at a birthday party, hanging out with friends, sitting in class, trying to finish homework, or even lying in bed trying to fall asleep. Suddenly, there’s that thought or stream of thoughts. The “What Ifs.” "What if something goes wrong?” The constant stream of negative thoughts runs through your head, and there is no ‘stop’ button

In my work with people of all ages, I see how easily anxious thoughts can hijack our attention. They interrupt our ability to be present, interfere with concentration, and sometimes make even the simplest tasks feel overwhelming. The problem isn't always the thought itself. It's what happens when we get stuck in the cycle of thinking, rethinking, analyzing, and overanalyzing. What do we do with all of that mental noise? Sometimes, the answer is surprisingly simple: Put it on paper.

There's Something Powerful About Putting Pen to Paper

Writing out our thoughts can be therapeutic, but we don't always need an audience. We live in a world where just about everything happens on a screen. We text, scroll, type, swipe, and communicate in abbreviations. Somewhere along the way, we seem to have lost the art of slowing down and writing by hand with pen and paper rather than texting or typing on a keyboard.

Journaling is more than writing down what happened during your day. It's an opportunity to slow your brain down long enough to process what's happening inside of it. The neuropsychological component of writing: When we journal, we're engaging multiple areas of our brain. We have to organize our thoughts, retrieve information, put feelings into words, sequence our ideas, and translate them into written language.

We're also engaging executive functioning skills, including working memory, organization, planning, and self-monitoring. There’s an emotional component. Sometimes we don't even realize how we're feeling until we start writing. A thought that seemed so big in our heads might look a little different once it's on paper. We may begin to recognize patterns, identify triggers, or realize that what we're worried about isn't necessarily what we're upset about. Writing allows us to pause, reflect, and look at our thoughts from a different perspective. It's not about having perfect handwriting, perfect grammar, or writing something profound. It's about permitting yourself to be honest.

We can remind ourselves, especially as parents, that we spend so much time filling our days. Our children's days are filled with school, homework, sports, activities, social commitments, and screens. Our own days are filled with work, responsibilities, errands, family obligations, and the never-ending to-do list. We're constantly moving from one thing to the next. But when do we stop? When do we give ourselves (and our children) the chance to slow down, reflect, and reconnect?

We talk a lot about helping children develop emotional regulation skills, but we forget children need opportunities to practice identifying and expressing what they're feeling. Journaling can be one of those opportunities. For younger children, it might mean drawing a picture, writing a few words, or having a parent help them put their feelings into sentences. For adolescents, it might be a private notebook where they can work through friendships, school stress, social pressures, and all those complicated feelings that come with growing up.

If you or your child aren't sure what to write, try starting with one of these:

Journaling isn't a magic cure for anxiety, and it doesn't mean that every worry will disappear once you put it on paper. But it can help create some distance between you and your thoughts. It can help you recognize patterns, process emotions, organize your thinking, and feel a little more in control. Most importantly, it gives you something we don't make enough time for anymore: uninterrupted time with yourself. So, put down the phone. Close the laptop. Grab a notebook and a pen.

You don't need to write a novel, sound intelligent, or even make sense. Just start writing because sometimes the best way to quiet the noise in your head is to give those thoughts somewhere else to go.

#4772. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4771. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

For a more elevated look, try a merino wool or cashmere hoodie, which instantly dress things up. When it comes to layering, the trick to dressing up a hoodie is balancing its relaxed feel with something more structured. Think a blazer, bomber, or denim jacket. Even a sleek leather jacket or wool coat can take things up a notch.

#4769. When Setting Boundaries Backfires

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Lisa was at the end of her tether. The demands of her life had started to weigh on her so heavily that she felt crushed under the burden of it all. Lisa came to me because she had difficulty getting out of bed in the morning; she felt numb, flat, and low most days, and nothing in her life gave her joy anymore.

She had three kids and had, through sheer grit and self-abandonment, built a successful business that allowed her to work from home, while her husband worked a highly demanding city job. She was responsible for all her kids’ activities, school runs, the house, and everything that came with it. When her mother became ill, and Lisa had to add regular hospital visits to her to-do list, something in her broke. She was done.

Lisa was suffering from burnout. She had been raised to be the “good daughter,” “good mother,” and “good wife,” and any departure from those self-assigned roles felt like a betrayal to the life she had built. In therapy, we started to work on Lisa just noticing her own feelings and needs, but it was difficult for her to stay with herself. Any stretch she made to step out of one of her roles, an all-mighty guilt force would pull her back in. If she looked after herself, her kids might suffer, her mum might be alone, her husband might feel more overwhelmed. Lisa felt stuck, and she was.

She got there in the end, but only because the alternative now felt untenable. She had been barely sleeping for months, and her body was under constant tension that she couldn’t switch off from anymore. She let go of bits of her to-do list; she asked her sister to check in on her mum and her husband to drop the kids off a few days a week. She started to create boundaries around her own capacity and communicated them to the family system around her. She felt elated. But neither of us was fully prepared for what happened next.

When Lisa’s husband realized that she was asking for permanent changes to their daily routine, he started picking fights, accusing her of being selfish and putting too much pressure on him. He invalidated her feelings and reminded her how much time off she had compared to him. Lisa’s children rebelled, and her sister became distant and stopped taking Lisa’s calls.

Lisa was devastated and felt completely unseen. She was stuck between her new and old self, unable to move forward in either direction. What was happening to her family? Why could they not understand what she was going through?

Families, according to Bowen’s family system theory, are deeply interconnected. If one person changes, the whole system has to change. Lisa setting boundaries for the first time triggered her family to push back because the easiest way for the whole system to regain equilibrium would be for Lisa to return to her overfunctioning self.

Lisa’s systems had grown around the role she had been playing in them. She had taken on most of the childcare responsibilities, and her husband’s and her children’s expectations were built around that. With Lisa playing her part, the system was in balance, seemingly. When Lisa changed the rules, the system tumbled out of kilter.

Bowen suggested that differentiation of the self in an emotionally interconnected system goes through several stages—the act of setting the boundary, the system pushing back, and the boundary having to be maintained in the face of that pushback so that the system can adapt. Bowen essentially postulated that, in a system under high pressure or anxiety, you cannot expect boundary setting to go smoothly. Pushback is a predictable step in achieving differentiation and also what makes “saying no” so unbelievably hard.

Most of Lisa’s therapy sessions from that point forward revolved around understanding whether Lisa wanted to continue in her marriage. Lisa’s guilt had kept her going for years. It had protected her from the very real possibility of a huge relational rupture with her partner and her family. But now, if her husband couldn’t see how much she was suffering, how could she be with him?

Bowen’s theory clues us in as to why change in Lisa’s family was so difficult, and it also reminds us that things are rarely as black and white as they seem at first glance. Lisa was self-employed, and setting boundaries for her had less impact on her job but saved her from burnout. Her husband’s boss, however, noticed him being late a few mornings and had a chat with him about his commitment to his role. Lisa’s husband suddenly felt helpless, and his anxiety became overwhelming. He blamed Lisa without thinking and pushed her further away.

When Lisa changed the rules, she and her husband had to re-evaluate their lives in fundamental ways. Lisa’s husband had been working in a job he hated for years because of the financial obligations of having three children. When Lisa and her husband were honest with each other, they realized that Lisa’s burnout had brought to light fissures in their family system that had been there for a long time. It took a lot of effort and honesty for them to rebuild a life that took both of their needs into account.

Other times, relationships will fall apart when one person steps out of their assigned role, and we have to be honest about how interconnected and dependent on each other we are as human beings. Boundary setting is not always as easy as our quick-fix culture would like us to believe. Saying no when your guilt has been keeping you overfunctioning for decades is empowering and freeing, but it will likely mean altering the relationships in your life, sometimes drastically.

If you are finding it hard to set boundaries, remind yourself that this is not meant to be easy. Seek professional help and always take small steps to give the systems around you and yourself a chance to adapt. True change is hard; don’t try to do it on your own.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Jenny Brown and Lauren Errington, ‘Bowen Family Systems Theory and Practice: Illustration and Critique Revisited’, Australian and New Zealand Journal of Family Therapy 45, no. 2 (2024): 135–55, https://doi.org/10.1002/anzf.1589

M. Calatrava et al., ‘Differentiation of Self: A Scoping Review of Bowen Family Systems Theory’s Core Construct’, Clinical Psychology Review 91 (February 2022): 102101, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2021.102101;

The Bowen Center for the Study of Family, 10 November 2026, https://www.thebowencenter.org.

#4768. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

#4767. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4766. Speeders just got lucky: the new Chevy police Silverado is NOT electric

Say what you will about America’s police forces, but they are loyal – often to each other, and always to their preferred brand of pursuit vehicle. And if the thin blue line of Chevy faithful won’t embrace the 750 hp electric Silverado because it’s powered by batteries, that can really only be called a win for the scofflaws they’re pursuing.

A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The 9C1 also features an available 2″ lift kit that retains the truck’s pursuit rating, up to 9,300 lbs. of towing capacity, and an available driver’s side LED spotlight.

If that all sounds somewhat pedestrian, it might be because Electrek readers are more familiar with the Silverado EV, which offers more than 750 hp in WOW mode and 775 lb-ft of torque at 0 rpm, along with a pessimistic EPA rating of just 478 miles – which, hilariously, is about the same “range” as the 16 mpg (combined) gas version, despite the EV packing nearly 350 additional horsepower, the ability to cruise in silence, and the significantly reduced maintenance and total cost of ownership costs of going electric.

Which, I guess, are all reasonably obvious things that nobody actually asked me about – and certainly nobody with a criminal justice degree and a statistically low LSAT score, so I’ll get back to talking about the truck, itself.

A massive, 16″ touchscreen display dominates the interior of the PPV, and was also touted as a standard feature (as it across Chevy’s civilian line), though if and how it would integrate with police department software isn’t clear – and my guess is that enforcement computing will continue to be an upfitter issue.

I don’t know why anyone would use a truck as a persuit vehicle? It seems reckless inefficient and ineffective.

Guess we are on the topic of us policing…

#4765. Can a Mental Health Crisis Ever Be a Gift?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Two years ago, I found myself locked in a county jail for four months because of threats I made while in a manic psychosis. I had spent almost a decade eluding treatment for my bipolar I disorder, and the consequences of that circumvention had caught up with me. Behind bars for the first time in my life, and surrounded by beige concrete, I took cold comfort in Nietzsche’s concept of amor fati, or love of one’s fate. Instead of accepting my fate, I thought of counterfactuals: What if I had accepted my diagnosis earlier? What if I had gone to the hospital instead of insisting I was fine?

Two years later, I find peace in a routine of stability and sobriety and writing and advocacy. I have a treatment plan that works for me, have rekindled a loving relationship with my mother after 10 years of estrangement, and have embarked on a career of mental health advocacy that grew out of the wreckage of a catastrophe.

Now, the impulse to tell a redemptive story is tempting. It would be easy, compelling, and even flattering to say that the illness was the price I had to pay for everything good that followed. A reckoning with the past invites the tantalizing questions: Can a mental health crisis be a gift? Who gets to decide?

In an essay from earlier this year, psychiatrist Awais Aftab narrates two recent accounts: although Tyler Alterman could not get out of bed for over a year, he now says that he is grateful for the depression that saved his life; Jazmine Russell considers her psychotic episode an inspiring lesson in how her life was once breaking her down. These narratives have real therapeutic value, since they translate the senseless suffering of psychic collapse into a language that one can speak confidently into the future.

I know their appeal. The remorse I feel, the memoir I’m writing, the advocacy talks I give—none of it could have come without the calamity that came before. Psychologists call this kind of change post-traumatic growth, and research suggests it is common.

It feels seductive to see mental health disorders as a type of evolutionary adaptation that confers advantages on a suffering soul. But as evolutionary psychiatrist Randolph Nesse points out, this is a fallacy. Low mood and anxiety may be useful defenses, but “diseases are not adaptations shaped by natural selection.” As Aftab explains, a symptom (such as a loss of sleep) can lead to positive changes in one’s life (such as improved sleep hygiene) without having been designed for it. A death of a loved one may alter the course of one’s life for the better, encouraging one to cherish remaining relationships, but no one with a straight face would call that death a gift.

In my case, I would be hard-pressed to find the good in my mania. While it felt like clarity, like the best version of me I had ever embodied, it made me cruel and selfish, and it cleared my life of family and friends.

While in jail and during my 10 months at a state psychiatric hospital, I tried to find meaning in my chaos. Whereas I once thought, I am a failure, I learned to reframe the global indictment into the more contained expression of I had failed. The failure supplied the raw material to craft something new. I took solace in Viktor Frankl’s expression of “the last of the human freedoms—to choose one’s attitude.” Edith Eger inspired me with her idea that “the opposite of depression is expression.”

Still, meaning-making was hardly a solitary act: my mother kept showing up to visit me, and read books on bipolar disorder and neuroscience alongside me; at the hospital, I met weekly with a caring psychologist who asked me about how I processed my shame. To call my illness and the decade of destruction it wrought a gift would be to credit it with my mother’s persistence and my psychologist’s curiosity, along with the arduous work I did myself.

But as I learned from my stay at that state hospital, not everyone has cognitive access to Frankl’s freedoms. My neighbor, whom I will call Johnnie, had spent decades at the institution, where he battled voices for what seemed like every hour of every day. He often interjected during our therapeutic groups with quirky one-liners. Rain tastes like Southern Comfort and moonshine. And that’s dangerous. Or I’m Johnnie, and today is a miracle, even with the rain.

Psychologist Steven Heine notes that intense trauma “can completely upend people’s meaning frameworks,” leaving some to “struggle, sometimes for decades.” The allure of a redemptive narrative is that it is written by a survivor, and hidden behind that appeal is a kind of survivorship bias. The very process of looking back on a past crisis, as Aftab says, distorts our perception of the crisis. While a crisis may be one route to change, it is rarely the best one. Telling someone in the middle of a psychotic episode, or a father waiting in an emergency room lobby, that their pain may turn out to be a gift risks romanticizing an episode, forcing a search on demand to find meaning in catastrophe.

Aftab provides a similar lesson for clinicians when he suggests that psychiatrists “should honor the patient’s meaning-making while being mindful of its fallibility.” For every person who can trumpet how a crisis saved their life, far too many, like Johnnie, are prisoners to illnesses that have given them nothing.

While I was initially drawn to the bravado of amor fati, I remained attached to it over time because it taught me the discipline of gratitude. I had the drive, determination, and education to make sense of a crippling mental illness whose riddle the mental health system seemed uninterested in helping me solve. I recovered because I read deeply about the illness that almost took my life, but I also recovered because I never felt alone: I had a mother who kept my memory alive for a decade, and who kept showing up for me because she believed in the promise of her son.

The redemptive arc—the notion that a mental health breakdown can be a breakthrough—is appealing to our quick-fix culture. But it is better to be honest: I can accept all the ugly that has happened, and even love the life it led to, without needing to claim that the illness taught me a necessary lesson in life.

Aftab, A. (2026, January 10). Can a psychiatric crisis save your life? Psychiatry at the Margins.

Eger, E. E. (2020). The Gift: 12 Lessons to Save Your Life. New York: Scribner.

Frankl, V. E. (2006). Man’s Search for Meaning. Boston: Beacon Press.

Heine, S. J. (2025, January 28). The curious relations between suffering and meaning. Psychology Today.

Nesse, R. M. (2023). Evolutionary psychiatry: foundations, progress and challenges. World Psychiatry, 22(2), 177–202.

#4764. Emideltide Keeps Getting a ‘No’ for Compounding. What’s the Problem?

Why the government’s renewed interest in peptides excludes this one.

THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION has not been shy about its pro-peptide stance. US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has pushed to make six popular yet unapproved peptides available for compounding to people with a prescription. A recent FDA advisory committee meeting voted in favor of adding six out of seven peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply.

Six out of seven. So what happened to that last peptide? Emideltide, also dubbed DSIP, is a peptide people have turned to for better sleep. And it was the only peptide the FDA advisory board voted against moving out of the Category 2 list—a substance considered to carry significant safety risks, with compounding pharmacies prohibited from making it. Here’s why.

EMIDELTIDE IS A nine-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits during electrically induced sleep in the late 1970s. Since its discovery, a synthetic peptide version has been administered via injection or a nasal spray.

Emideltide reportedly helps you fall asleep faster and extend the time spent in deep sleep. It’s also been used to avoid waking up multiple times throughout the night and anecdotal reports online have mentioned more vivid, Inception–like lucid dreaming. With better sleep, people online using emideltide have mentioned feeling less stress, more refreshed upon waking, and faster recovery after a grueling workout.

MOST RESEARCH LOOKING into the peptide’s role in sleep, however, took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed findings.

For example, a 1984 case study reported on a 35-year-old guy with 10 years of narcolepsy who had reduced sleep attacks, less daytime napping, and more alertness with weekly emideltide injections administered in the morning.

One clinical trial had 16 people take an emideltide injection or a placebo while measuring how long it took for them to fall asleep once they’re tucked into bed. People who had an emideltide injection said they felt more tired and actually went to sleep quicker than the placebo group. That should be great except when they repeated the experiment a second night, the placebo group knocked out quicker than the peptide group.

Another study in 1992 found the peptide helped chronic insomniacs feel less tired. However, there was such little difference in the time it took to fall asleep and stay asleep in the emideltide group versus the placebo group. The authors of the 1992 study said any small improvements with the peptide were probably “due to an incidental change in the placebo group” and “not likely to be of major therapeutic benefit.”

BEYOND SLEEP, EMIDELTIDE has been explored in animal studies for potentially protecting against cancer and improving motor ability after stroke. Another realm of interest is how emideltide might help with curbing withdrawal after addiction.

A 1984 study found emideltide injections helped reduce the severity of opioid withdrawal symptoms in 97 percent of people with addiction along with alcohol withdrawal symptoms in 87 percent of people with alcohol addiction. Although more peptide injections were needed in people with opiate addiction.

In 1998, researchers gave a single injection of emideltide to seven people with opioid dependence. While they reported improvements in opioid withdrawal, the team also noted “it remains an open question whether DSIP could be an effective alternative detoxification approach.” Some of the issues were the small sample size, lack of a placebo group for proper comparison, and that each person knew they were getting an emideltide injection. The lack of randomization makes it hard to say for sure that a treatment actually worked or if people subjectively felt better because they knew they were getting treatment.

WE KNOW EMIDELTIDE doesn’t act like a sedative that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

The peptide is often considered a sleep-regulator rather than a suppressant. We know emideltide doesn’t act like a sedative or sleeping pill that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

One possible mechanism is that the peptide increases delta-wave activity. These are your slowest brain waves at 0.5 to 4 Hz that are indicative of deep sleep. Deep sleep is linked to better memory, energy, and all that good stuff you get from a good night’s sleep. There may also be some neuroendocrine effects going on that could explain why people feel calm enough to pass out. A small study back in the ’80s injected a single dose of emideltide in 11 guys and found lower levels of ACTH, a hormone that stimulates your adrenal glands to release the stress hormone cortisol (though this mechanism has been disputed).

The FDA advisory meeting relied on studies that focused on emideltide’s cross-talk with the opioid system in the brain. While the peptide doesn’t directly interact with opioid receptors, evidence points to emideltide somehow being able to trigger the release of endorphins. This may also provide painkiller properties (which is why it’s been proposed as a way to suppress alcohol and opioid withdrawal syndrome).

EMIDELTIDE WILL PROBABLY stay banned—and found only through the sketchy gray market—because there’s not enough information to know if emideltide might do more harm than good.

Since emideltide interacts with the opioid system, there is a possibility that it could lead to addiction. Right now, there are no animal or human studies that prove emideltide wouldn’t worsen addictive behaviors.

There’s also not enough data on whether repeated emideltide use would cause other safety issues. While the small sleep trials did not report any serious side effects, withdrawal studies noted headaches, nausea, and vertigo. After the second injection, some had low blood pressure although the researchers also said it’s unclear whether those symptoms were because of the peptide or from withdrawal altogether.

#4763. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4762. Bigger, badder Section 179 tax deduction could POWER UP fleet electrification [update]

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers, it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks, electric vocational trucks, battery electric reefer trailers, and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, magic pixie dust, anything else.

There’s been some additional movement on the tax front since our original article, too. Earlier this year, the IRS issued Notice 2026-11, providing additional guidance on the permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025. That means that eligible businesses might be able to combine Section 179 expensing with bonus depreciation when ordering qualifying fleet equipment – and ordering is the key word. The IRS has specific rules for determining when equipment is considered acquired under a written, binding contract, and your tax professional and truck dealer can probably help you figure out a way to make those rules work in your favor.

You can check out the original article (with a few corrections sprinkled in to align with the latest guidance from Notice 2026-11 and Publication 946) below. Give it a read, read the disclaimer twice, then let us know what you think in the comments.

After the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (Section 45W) expired on September 30, the “experts” rushed out predictions of an EV sales slowdown in Q4. But, with over 6,800 pages in the Internal Revenue Code still in play, a turbocharged Section 179 tax deduction could still power a strong year for commercial EVs.

The One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 gutted America’s energy independence goals and ensuring its auto industry would fall even further behind the Chinese in the EV race, but the loss of Section 45W wasn’t the only change written into the IRS’ rulebook. Section 179, an immediate expense reduction that business owners can take on depreciable equipment assets, has been made significantly more powerful for 2025.

The section 179 expense deduction is limited to such items as cars, office equipment, business machinery, and computers. This speedy deduction can provide substantial tax relief for business owners who are purchasing startup equipment.

The revised Section 179 tax credit (or, more accurately, expense reduction) allows for a 100% deduction for equipment purchases has doubled to $2.5 million, with a phase-out kicking in at $4 million of capital investments that drops to zero at $6.5 million. That can be applied to new and used vehicles, as well as charging infrastructure, battery energy storage systems, specialized tools, and more (as long as they’re new to you).

“But wait,” as they say. “There’s more!” A revised Section 168(k) also allows for bonus depreciation on eligible equipment and property, accelerating depreciation for a reduced tax burden.

Section 179 and bonus depreciation aren’t mutually exclusive, either, which means that businesses don’t have to exceed the Section 179 spending cap to be able to take advantage of both. A fleet operator can elect to expense a portion of a qualifying vehicle or equipment purchase under Section 179, then apply bonus depreciation to the remaining eligible basis.

With 100% bonus depreciation restored for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, that combination could allow businesses to deduct the entire qualifying business-use cost of an electric truck or other commercial equipment in the first year, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and limitations.

It’s a bit convoluted (what good tax code isn’t?), but these tax incentives are great for businesses looking to buy enough electric equipment assets to exceed the Section 179 spending limit – and, given the new Uber/Tesla semi truck purchase plan, the continued growth of the electric terminal tractor market, and the willingness of several utilities to incentivize both electric commercial vehicles and the deployment of smart EV charging infrastructure, that number may be bigger than you think.

Tax law is weird. Not only are there Federal tax laws and rules that need to be followed, but state and even local county and city rules, as well. As such, you want to make sure they don’t get you the way the got Capone.

Even worse, your favorite journalist (Hi!) is probably an idiot. Get a certified accountant and tax law expert to help walk you through the dirtier details of your specific scenario – but don’t let the complexity of human interaction slow you down, either. The really rich guys you know pay pennies on the tax dollar compared to you and me, because they’re not afraid to ask their accountants for help.

As a tax CPA, I cringe when I see "Sec 179" and the word "credit" put together. It is grossly inaccurate to say that Sec 179 is a tax credit.

Sec 179 and bonus depreciation are nothing new. OBBBA just raised the 179 maximum up, but the deductibility, specifically for heavy vehicles like semis, is unchanged.

The TL;DR version, though, is this: there’s still plenty of incentives out there for fleet operators looking to electrify their operations.

SOURCES | IMAGES: Equipment World, Investopedia, Volvo.

#4761. How Curiosity and Preparing Well Can Bring Peace in Divorce

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

This article is the second in a series that provides practical takeaways from three pioneers in family conflict resolution, who, through their decades of experience, have become internationally respected peacemakers and trainers of families and divorce professionals. Click here to read the first article.

Families of gray divorce, which refers to couples 50 and older, often become mired in conflict and struggle with effective communication. Family members can feel pulled to align with a parent or sibling. Not being able to listen to understand each other can lead to emotional outbursts, pain, anger, fights, and becoming estranged.

In recognition of Conflict Resolution Day, which is observed internationally on the third Thursday of October every year, and of the approaching holiday season that promotes giving thanks and peace throughout the world, I spoke with Jacinta Gallant, Canadian family lawyer, mediator, conflict educator, and international trainer.

A former client stopped Jacinta in a grocery store with words that show why her approach works. I’ll share them later in the interview.

Carol Hughes: Looking back over your career, what experiences or realizations led you to believe there was a better way for families to resolve the conflicts of divorce?

Jacinta Gallant: As a lawyer advocate, I had my share of “wins” and “losses,” but soon realized that most families lost in an adversarial justice system. I decided I could no longer use my talent to make things worse, so I became a mediator. In this role, I got to know both “sides” and was able to explore what each family needed for healthy coparenting and better outcomes for children.

This was a pivotal change for my career. I felt far more satisfied, even joyful, in my work. The missing piece arrived with the development of interdisciplinary collaborative practice, which brings together lawyers and mental health professionals to truly meet the needs of each family. Many lawyers are not natural “team” players, but I am—and I find it so rewarding working with other disciplines in a shared mission to support healthy families and communities.

CH: You have studied conflict resolution for decades. What are the important points that family members need to understand about what conflict is and how to resolve it?

JG: I wish the public knew that their choice of lawyer and the approach they take will have a profound impact on their family for a very long time. There are rare occasions when parents or children need the protection of family court. But almost all families don’t. Most parents don’t realize the harm that will come to their family in an adversarial court proceeding, and soon after they decide to separate, they “lawyer up.” I hate that term!

The “family justice” system is built on an adversarial model that applies facts to law and is ill-suited to managing relational dynamics and meeting children’s needs. The best family lawyers will say that therapeutic support is more important than anything else in the early stage of separation. They will acknowledge that it is almost impossible to provide firm and relevant initial advice because more information is needed. Despite this, traditional family lawyers often revert to advocating and focus on protecting their own client. That “zealous advocacy” can ignore the deeper needs of the whole family—especially the children.

CH: At some point, you chose to extend your work beyond helping individual families to writing, teaching, and training other professionals. What inspired you to broaden your reach, and what did you hope would change as a result?

JG: Most family lawyers and judges really care. I thought if I could help train more lawyers in conflict resolution, the families and their communities would benefit. I took time out in 2018 to study the insight approach to conflict, and it changed everything for me. Bringing this to the legal and mental health community has been the most rewarding aspect of my career. Drs. Cheryl Picard and Kenneth Melchin explain the distinguishing features of the insight approach in a paper listed in the references below.

CH: After all you have witnessed and learned over the course of your career, what gives you hope about the future of how families experience and resolve divorce conflict?

JG: I met a client in the grocery store last week, and she said, “It’s happening! You said we would meet someday in the future, and I would be OK. And I am.”

She gave me a hug and was so full of appreciation. What did I do that made the difference? I listened and demonstrated a sincere desire to understand her before giving her any “advice.” I dropped my “know-it-all” mentality (an occupational hazard for lawyers) and harnessed the power of curiosity. My curiosity grounded us both and led to insights.

My clients leave our office feeling better than when they walked in. I now conduct my initial client consultations with more listening, less telling. This leads to better communication and better outcomes.

CH: Your Our Family in Two Homes and Our Family in a Few Homes workbooks emphasize helping families prepare before they begin creating solutions. What have you learned about how preparation shapes families’ experience and resolution of divorce conflict?

JG: In 2019, I asked my clients what it was like to work with me. I wanted to improve their experience. They thought I asked great questions, and they often had better answers after they left my office. They appreciated our deeper (non-law) conversations but often worried about how much it was costing them. And they said they wish they had been better prepared for each stage of our work together.

So, I poured their generous feedback and my emerging understanding of the insight approach to conflict into creating client preparation tools that are now being used with families around the world. The resources are intentionally curious—meant to elicit the client’s own discoveries about themselves at a time when most people are so stressed they have no curiosity!

The preparation engages them in a safe learning experience that opens their minds to more possibilities. They engage in self-reflection without resistance because they can do this on their own time and on their own dime. With this preparation, when they meet with their chosen divorce professional, they feel more grounded and ready to engage. We have had such a positive response that we have created a public version so that every family can access the resources, often before they call a lawyer. Choose a collaborative lawyer or mediator.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Picard, C., Melchin, K. (2022). Insight Mediation Working Paper #1: Four Distinguishing Features. Insight Today. https://www.insighttodayonline.com/blog/h18evcq5si3b9yrun85f3kf9plyl4v

Gallant, J. (2019). Our Family in Two Homes. www.intwohomes.com

Gallant, J. (2020). Our Family in a Few Homes. www.intwohomes.com
